turns.en: What does building software look like inside of Entropik today? Caitlyn is the head of engineering for platform at the company. Today's episode will be about Entropik and you probably heard that they rebuilt their version control system because the existing one could not take the increased load from AI agents. A trail can be spread across multiple repos so the change to your backend and your web app gets reviewed once. With a trail, you can configure customized evals like code reviews, security reviews, slot reviews, and others. They look like a heads-up display in an airplane and score your work on every push. And you can see how each agent runs or passes your user-defined gates and decides when you merge based on these. The point is that you control when you allow agents to merge the code, like only merging after a human review or after all gates pass. turns.zh: 是的，当然。这是我们自去年年底到今年年初以来一直在思考的事情，当时我们开始看到请求量真的真的真的激增。我认为尤其是今年早些时候，对我们团队来说一件有趣的事情是，我们投放了一个超级碗广告，你知道你投放超级碗广告，这是一个经典的工程问题，你必须小心你会看到什么样的峰值。所以再次因为我们所有的应用都运行在 Messages API 上，它非常像是服务一切可能峰值的层。比如你知道超级碗广告可能不会导致某人当场打开笔记本电脑构建 API 集成，但你可能会选择下载我们的移动应用并试一试，而这一切仍然通过 API 运行。所以我们开始看到请求量真的真的上升，在那段时间，嗯，你知道我们运行的 CPU 集群开始变得相当紧张。所以这真的很有趣，因为在我的职业生涯中，我认为对大多数人来说直到最近，CPU 是一种资源，你知道，你可以随心所欲地自动扩展。你得付钱，但如果你想要更多，你可以得到更多。而这是我们开始或我个人开始感受到的第一次，你知道，我们想要从云中获得更多，而对话比以往任何时候都更难。

And models were starting to get better and it was maybe okay that we didn't have people in um the team who had done a lot of rust development previously.
turns.zh: 所以，嗯，实际上，你说得很有趣，我们已经开始用 Go 构建一些服务。所以实际上，在我们运行的所有服务中，我们有一些 Python。嗯，现在不多了。我们大部分已经替换了。我们去年某个时候就开始用 Go 构建一些新服务，我们开始做经典的，比如我们有一个巨大的单体应用。让我们做更多的面向服务的架构。当我们构建新服务时，我们希望这些服务是什么样子？非常经典的工程辩论，你选择什么？嗯，当时选择 Go 是因为，你知道，模型还没有到语言选择完全不重要的地步，你知道吗？你仍然想要一些对开发者友好的东西来开发。所以 Go 被选中是因为它在效率和开发者体验的频谱上处于一个更好的位置。然后变得有趣的是，因为 Anthropic 所有系统中最需要高性能的部分，人们开始追求我们应该更进一步，对吧？而模型开始变得更好，也许我们团队中没有做过很多 Rust 开发的人也是可以的。

turns.en: And we came all the way to Rust as the new-age interesting language that you could choose that would be really efficient and give us all of those wins, but maybe it was okay that we didn't quite have tons of Rust developers in the room because the models had gotten good enough that the implementation details could be more handled by the models.
turns.zh: 我们一路选定了 Rust 作为新时代有趣的语言，它能提供高效率并带来所有这些优势，但也许当时没有大量 Rust 开发者也没关系，因为模型已经足够好，实现细节可以更多地交给模型处理。

turns.en: Yeah, and I understand, correct me if I'm wrong, that the thing with performance in Rust is taking out assembly because that's chip-specific and you would need to rewrite it every single time. But outside of that, C++ gives you the most efficiency because you can have pretty much full control over the memory, over how you allocate things. And apparently with Rust, you can have on par with it, but you can be memory safe. C++ is not memory safe, but in return you need to understand things like the borrow checker. And you cannot do certain things. At compile time the language stops you, but new engineers often get confused because it's really frustrating. And then everything else, all the languages they have at least one small abstraction layer that will mean that their performance will be slightly worse, but it'll be more developer productive. Is this like—
turns.zh: 是的，如果我理解错了请纠正我：Rust 在性能方面的问题在于要移除汇编，因为汇编是芯片特定的，每次都需要重写。但除此之外，C++ 能给你最高的效率，因为你可以几乎完全控制内存、控制如何分配。而显然用 Rust 你可以达到同等水平，同时还能内存安全。C++ 不是内存安全的，但作为回报你需要理解借用检查器之类的东西。而且你不能做某些事情。在编译时语言会阻止你，但新工程师常常感到困惑，因为这真的很令人沮丧。然后其他所有语言至少有一层小的抽象层，这意味着它们的性能会稍差，但开发效率更高。这是不是像——

turns.en: Yes, exactly. So, I think there was just like a really nice tradeoff in there between we were going for the most efficiency that we could possibly get without some of the—I don't know how many engineers would have quit if we were like we're doing in C++ now. But I think Rust was interesting to a lot of people as something that accounted for some of these tradeoffs and those foot guns that you kind of talked about that can be really frustrating are things that we could rely on models to deal with some of those things for us. And so there were definitely growing pains at first when we first started doing this and people didn't really know what they were doing yet and half the battle is Claude helps you write the code, the other half of the battle is Claude helps you learn what code is being written and what's even happening. And so in that world I think we found what felt like a good tradeoff and I think a lot of people on our team would say that faster than they expected to they got really comfortable with Rust and with developing in Rust. The same thing happened with Go by the way. When we first started building in Go we didn't really have too many people who had done so in the past. We had a couple but people were really nervous about this. They were like you know I was a Ruby developer or I was a Python developer or whatever it might be and this was a new language and even then at the time a year ago when the models weren't quite as good people felt like really quickly they were able to get comfortable and learn the paradigms and get started. And I think that's one of the magical things about these models is people are like oh the models are writing all the code and so it doesn't really matter if you understand all the details, but actually you can understand the details if you want to and it's easier to learn them because the models will help you do that part too.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。所以我认为这里有一个非常好的权衡：我们追求尽可能高的效率，而不必——我不知道如果像现在用 C++ 那样会有多少工程师辞职。但我认为 Rust 对很多人来说很有趣，因为它考虑了一些权衡，而你提到的一些令人沮丧的陷阱，我们可以依靠模型来处理。所以一开始肯定有成长的烦恼，人们还不太知道自己在做什么，一半的战斗是 Claude 帮你写代码，另一半的战斗是 Claude 帮你了解正在写什么代码以及发生了什么。所以在这个世界里，我们找到了一个感觉不错的权衡，我们团队很多人会说他们比预期更快地熟悉了 Rust 并用 Rust 开发。顺便说一句，Go 也一样。当我们刚开始用 Go 构建时，并没有太多人以前做过。我们有几个人，但人们真的很紧张。他们会说，你知道，我以前是 Ruby 开发者或 Python 开发者之类的，这是一门新语言，即使在一年前模型还没那么好时，人们也很快就能适应、学习范式并开始上手。我认为这些模型的神奇之处之一就是，人们会说哦模型在写所有代码，所以你是否理解所有细节并不重要，但实际上如果你想，你可以理解细节，而且更容易学习，因为模型也会帮你做那部分。

turns.en: And how did you approach this? Is it more of a hand-wavy like okay go ahead and implement this and this and then you're not going to look at the code or as you say you want to learn, you want to at least understand and then validate and then later trust the certain things that you can trust. What's your approach?
turns.zh: 那你是怎么处理的？是更随意地说好吧，继续实现这个和这个，然后你就不看代码了，还是像你说的你想学习，你想至少理解然后验证，然后后来信任某些你可以信任的东西。你的方法是什么？

turns.en: Yeah, I think the natural inclination for any engineer is you want to learn a little bit. You want to be able to look at the code if you have to and have somewhat of a sense for what's going on. I think at the end of the day, if you're someone who used to write code by hand in any of these languages, it's not like the most foreign insane thing to look at Rust code and figure out what's going on. And so I think for the most part, if I had to put a percentage on it, I would say 75% it's like the model is going to write the code and understanding the exact syntax maybe doesn't matter. But then 25% I would say is just like an engineer's natural inclination is I kind of want to understand what's going on here. And so you find yourself asking the model questions and figuring out a bit about what it's actually writing and what's actually happening. And then you get to a point where you're just more comfortable than somebody who's coming in totally blind. You can see it and generally understand what matters.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为任何工程师的自然倾向都是想学一点。你希望必要时能看看代码，对正在发生的事情有所感觉。我认为归根结底，如果你曾经用这些语言中的任何一种手写代码，那么看 Rust 代码并弄清楚发生了什么并不是最陌生疯狂的事情。所以我认为大部分情况下，如果非要给个百分比，我会说 75% 是模型会写代码，理解确切的语法可能不重要。但另外 25% 我会说就是工程师的自然倾向，我有点想理解这里发生了什么。所以你会问模型问题，了解它实际在写什么以及实际发生了什么。然后你会达到一个比完全盲目的人更舒服的状态。你能看到它并大致理解什么重要。

turns.en: Yeah, and I guess you see the high-level structure. You might decide I want to learn. I want to understand what these few lines do because then you're like you want to understand. Is it like a trust but verify thing-ish?
turns.zh: 是的，我猜你看到高层结构。你可能会决定我想学习。我想理解这几行是做什么的，因为然后你就想理解。这有点像信任但验证吗？

But I think for the most part, it's like the actual implementation details, the nitty-gritty syntax of how exactly the code gets written just doesn't matter nearly as much anymore, especially as this year has gone on and the models have gotten better throughout this year. You can trust much more that as long as you are really clear about the intent that you have with what you want code to do, that the model will write the code better than you probably would have yourself.
turns.zh: 有点像。但我的意思是，如果我试图声称大多数情况下你并不真的需要理解每一个细节，那我就是在撒谎，对吧？就像我认为工程师有点想这样做，你花一点时间，就稍微了解一点。但我认为大部分情况下，实际的实现细节，代码具体如何编写的细微语法，已经不那么重要了，尤其是随着今年过去，模型在今年变得越来越好。你可以更加信任，只要你对代码要做什么的意图非常清晰，模型会比你本人写得更好。

turns.en: One reason developers were frustrated with Rust, but also it was a very powerful thing, it's the language that has the most compile-time checks. So as a dev, you would—when I had Alice Ryhl here from the Rust team, she was saying how developers are really often like fighting the borrow checker and fighting Rust because their code will not compile. You put a lot of effort into it because there's all these feedback loops, but when you compile, she said Rust is becoming very popular because there's fewer bugs in Rust because there's a lot more compile-time checks, meaning if your code compiles, there's a whole category of bugs that is near impossible unless you use the unsafe keyword, which you shouldn't—I mean don't use it and then you'll be fine.
turns.zh: 开发者对 Rust 感到沮丧的一个原因，但也是它非常强大的地方，是它拥有最多的编译时检查。所以作为开发者，你会——当我邀请 Rust 团队的 Alice Ryhl 来时，她说开发者经常像在对抗借用检查器、对抗 Rust，因为他们的代码无法编译。你投入了很多努力，因为有所有这些反馈循环，但当你编译时，她说 Rust 正变得非常流行，因为 Rust 中的 bug 更少，因为有更多的编译时检查，这意味着如果你的代码编译通过，有一整类 bug 几乎不可能出现，除非你使用 unsafe 关键字，你不应该——我的意思是不要用它，然后你就没事了。

turns.en: Do you see this as well, that this is a reason for Rust to become more popular? Do the models get to iterate more, or just give you stuff that actually—there's a whole host of things you don't need to work for, for example, you don't need to worry about memory safety anymore.
turns.zh: 你是否也认为，这也是 Rust 变得更受欢迎的一个原因？模型能迭代更多吗，还是只是给你一些东西，实际上——有很多事情你不需要再操心了，比如你不再需要担心内存安全了。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And I think that's a lot of—I don't know—just things that you accomplish with models and things that you accomplish with agents. The more you can get it to be verifiable—you know, in a world of non-determinism, as long as you can get stuff to be verifiable, you're in a really, really great spot. And that's just one of the really nice things about this: okay, great, sure, you have more compile-time checks, and if you're writing code by hand and going through a really slow iteration loop to get your code to compile, that would be annoying. But in a world where you're not really even paying attention and the model is doing it, the agent is doing it, then that's great because you do have more trust in what you end up with once it gets there and it gets something working.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我认为这很大程度上——我不知道——就是模型能帮你完成的事情，以及智能体能帮你完成的事情。你越能让它变得可验证——你知道，在一个非确定性的世界里，只要你能让东西变得可验证，你就处于一个非常非常好的位置。而这正是这件事的一个好处：好吧，当然，你有更多的编译时检查，如果你手写代码，并且要经历一个非常缓慢的迭代循环才能让代码编译通过，那会很烦人。但在一个你甚至不太关注、模型在做、智能体在做的世界里，那就很棒，因为一旦它到达那个状态并让东西跑起来，你对最终结果会有更多的信任。

turns.en: So let's go to the trust. So okay, API, we will write parts of it in Rust. How did you slice and dice it, and then how did you trust it? Testing, verification, rolling out to production.
turns.zh: 那我们来谈谈信任。好吧，API，我们会用 Rust 写一部分。你是怎么拆分和处理的，然后你是怎么信任它的？测试、验证、上线到生产环境。

turns.en: Yeah, so the original plan was going to be, you know, like splice off pieces of the system and rewrite those in Rust. And then, uh, part of the way through getting started on doing that—and obviously that was a pretty slow undertaking—um, part of the way through doing that, um, I had a new senior engineer join my team and he kind of came in and he was like, hear me out. What if all at once? What if we do it—and he had kind of called it like great leap style. And the idea behind that was, what if we just stand up a basically like fork of the codebase and just like do that whole thing in Rust. Then you can kind of have this Python front door, right? Like a request comes in, there's like a really thin Python front door that can route a request through the Python system and then run a shadow through the Rust system. And then what's really interesting about that is that what really matters is making sure that the output you're getting is the same.
turns.zh: 是的，所以最初的计划是，你知道，就像把系统的一部分切出来，然后用 Rust 重写那些部分。然后，呃，在开始做这件事的过程中——显然那是一项相当缓慢的工程——嗯，在做的过程中，嗯，我有一个新的高级工程师加入了我的团队，他进来说，听我说。如果一次性全部搞定呢？如果我们这样做——他称之为“大跃进”式的做法。背后的想法是，如果我们直接建立一个基本上是代码库的分支，然后用 Rust 做整个事情。然后你可以有一个 Python 前门，对吧？就像一个请求进来，有一个非常薄的 Python 前门，可以将请求路由通过 Python 系统，然后通过 Rust 系统运行一个影子。然后真正有趣的是，真正重要的是确保你得到的输出是相同的。

turns.en: The same.
turns.zh: 相同的。

turns.en: Exactly. And then iterating until, you know, having the model say in any given day, how many of these requests were different between Rust and Python and iterate. The two big challenges that we had with that—well, the real one big challenge is we don't look at people's problems, we don't look at people's completions. And so if you had a difference, how do you know what about it is different between Python and Rust and how do you know how to fix it if we can't actually look at any of the data that is flowing through the system?
turns.zh: 没错。然后迭代，直到，你知道，让模型每天说，这些请求中有多少在 Rust 和 Python 之间是不同的，然后迭代。我们遇到的两个大挑战——嗯，真正的一个大挑战是，我们不看用户的问题，我们不看用户的补全。所以如果你有差异，你怎么知道 Python 和 Rust 之间有什么不同，如果我们实际上不能查看流经系统的任何数据，你怎么知道如何修复它？

turns.en: Oh, I see what you mean. So you're saying that because of data privacy and sensitivity and the way it works, if you would get a difference, you cannot just say like give me the raw data and I will debug. You just—it's impossible by—Okay. Okay.
turns.zh: 哦，我明白你的意思了。所以你是说，由于数据隐私和敏感性以及它的运作方式，如果你遇到差异，你不能只是说给我原始数据，我来调试。你就是——这不可能，因为——好吧。好吧。

turns.en: So that's really interesting, right? Cuz like—
turns.zh: 所以这真的很有趣，对吧？因为——

turns.en: That makes it more challenging.
turns.zh: 这让它更具挑战性。

turns.en: Right. Right. Cuz the whole thing that we were trying to do was just say like we could get this really clean if we get all the way to a place where 100% of the time you run the request through the Python system and the Rust system and you get the same output. We can't actually verify the details of those things. And so the first thing that we did was say like right up until the layer where something is like going down into inference, make sure that that is the same. And then the second thing that we did was on the way back out, just check token counts. The token counts are the same. Yeah, exactly. Then you kind of know um that it's the same. But then, you know, you still get into these places where you have these tiny differences and it's much, much, much harder when you can't look at the raw data. And so the team had to think about, you know, what are all the different ways that we can figure out what might be different between these two systems. And ultimately, I think it just came down to a lot of uh, you know, like how do we look at again just like right up until the—before something goes down into inference. And that's like really the meat of this system. And so in all of that, you know, you can see what's going on, and it's much easier to figure out what could be wrong. But that was how it worked, was basically just like iterating day over day on take the percentage of difference between Python and Rust and like drive it down, drive it down, drive it down until a place where it was um, you know, like near perfect, right? And then you say, okay, great, let's start rolling out the Rust system. And what we did was for a while we still had that Python front door because if for whatever reason we ran into a bug with the Rust system or like, you know, we refused to—the system refused to process a request for whatever reason it threw an error, you could always just fall back to the Python system. And so it would be a little bit slower, but that's better than just not getting a response at all. Um, and so that was kind of how we did it until we got comfortable enough to rip out that front door.
turns.zh: 对。对。因为我们试图做的整个事情就是，如果我们能达到一个地方，100% 的情况下你通过 Python 系统和 Rust 系统运行请求，并且得到相同的输出，我们就能让这件事非常干净。我们实际上无法验证那些细节。所以我们做的第一件事是，直到某个东西进入推理层之前，确保那部分是相同的。然后我们做的第二件事是，在返回的路上，只检查 token 数量。token 数量是相同的。是的，没错。然后你就知道，嗯，它是相同的。但然后，你知道，你仍然会遇到这些地方，有微小的差异，而当你不能查看原始数据时，这就难得多得多得多。所以团队不得不思考，你知道，我们能找出这两个系统之间可能有什么不同的所有不同方式。最终，我认为这归结为很多，呃，你知道，就像我们如何再次查看，就像直到——在某个东西进入推理之前。而这真的是这个系统的核心。所以在所有这些中，你知道，你可以看到发生了什么，找出可能出错的地方要容易得多。但这就是它的工作方式，基本上就是日复一日地迭代，取 Python 和 Rust 之间的差异百分比，然后把它降下来，降下来，降下来，直到一个地方，嗯，你知道，接近完美，对吧？然后你说，好吧，太好了，让我们开始推出 Rust 系统。我们做的是，有一段时间我们仍然保留那个 Python 前门，因为如果由于某种原因我们遇到了 Rust 系统的 bug，或者像，你知道，我们拒绝——系统由于某种原因拒绝处理请求并抛出错误，你总是可以回退到 Python 系统。所以它会慢一点，但总比完全得不到响应好。嗯，所以这就是我们做的方式，直到我们足够舒服地移除那个前门。

turns.en: And then you didn't look at the code generated all that much, like cuz usually with a migration you typically often be, you know, rewrite some part, you do a code review, you often have a testing layer, like a unit or integration testing layer that gives you a fallback. But obviously you still do what you say is the shadow, the shadowing, that is the ultimate source of truth. But you were just able to just like sleep through this like, oh, let's see how we ported the business logic.
turns.zh: 然后你并没有太多地查看生成的代码，因为通常迁移时，你通常会，你知道，重写一些部分，你做代码审查，你通常有一个测试层，比如单元或集成测试层，给你一个回退。但显然你仍然做了你说的影子，影子测试，那是最终的真相来源。但你就能像睡一觉一样度过这个，就像，哦，让我们看看我们是如何移植业务逻辑的。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly, which is kind of crazy. But I think that's the world that we live in now is as long as you can really boil something down to like make it verifiable in some way, then you don't have to look at every single line of Rust code that's getting written. And I think in this case actually, because of the nature of this system and how central it is and how important it was to get things right, I think more so than you might think, we ended up with engineers like getting into the details of the code and figuring out what might need to be fixed. If you were to ask the team, they would probably say something like 80% of the pull requests that got opened by agents, they didn't like deeply read through all of the code that had gotten written. And then I would say like 20% probably is where, you know, you were running into issues, you were trying to get something perfectly right and they kind of had to dig deep into the details and and understand what was going on with the code.
turns.zh: 是的，没错，这有点疯狂。但我认为这就是我们现在生活的世界，只要你能真正把某件事归结为某种可验证的方式，那么你就不必查看正在编写的每一行 Rust 代码。而且我认为在这种情况下，实际上，由于这个系统的性质、它的核心地位以及把事情做对的重要性，我认为比你想象的更多，我们最终让工程师深入代码细节，找出可能需要修复的地方。如果你问团队，他们可能会说，大约 80% 由智能体打开的拉取请求，他们并没有深入阅读所有已编写的代码。然后我会说大约 20% 可能是你遇到问题的地方，你试图把某件事做到完美，他们不得不深入细节，理解代码发生了什么。

turns.en: And now that we have the new system, like with the old system when you know it was written by hand, like it's typical that there are a few engineers who've been there for a long time who just understand the whole structure.
turns.zh: 现在有了这个新系统，就像旧系统是手写的时候，通常会有几位待了很久的工程师，他们就是理解整个结构。

turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Sometimes better places you will have documentation. We know it gets outdated, but better places especially for critical systems there's like up-to-date documentation. How has that changed with this new system?
turns.zh: 有时候好一点的地方会有文档。我们知道它会过时，但在好一点的地方，尤其是关键系统，会有最新的文档。有了这个新系统，情况发生了怎样的变化？

turns.en: Yeah, one of the funny things about this is because of the nature of Anthropic, you know again, we only first had an API like three years ago or so, right? And that had started with a really small team and the team had grown so quickly and the system had started to take on tons of load so quickly. In that time, we didn't exactly have perfect documentation of the Python system that we had, which is one of the things that I guess made this whole thing a little more challenging. It's not like we could say take this documentation and follow it and build a new system. And so from that perspective, I think we've always been and continue to be in a world where like the code itself for the most part is the documentation for the agents that are working on it. But I think something when it comes to the system design and how all these pieces fit together, it's been really cool to see how new engineers join and they're like, okay, I have to wrap my head around this system and be ready to work on it. That part has changed a lot because it used to be you'd ask someone to get at a whiteboard with you, right? And kind of draw the boxes and arrows and learn what was going on and maybe there were diagrams that were kind of out there that you could study and learn about what was going on. But now we see people join and the thing they do is they just ask Claude, like tell me how this thing works. And often you'll get something that's like an interactive application with not just boxes and arrows but really just like a rendering of the system where you can click through and say like, okay here's kind of how this piece of the system interacts with this other piece of the system. And anyone can learn the way that they want to learn, right? Like if they want to have this interactive application that they can click through deeply, or if they want to just have like docs that they can read through that will teach them things, right, or if they wanted to be like video style or podcast style, right, like you can have Claude make you any of those things in order to help you learn the system. And that's been one of the really cool things about how people have all done their own thing to learn what's going on.
turns.zh: 是的，有趣的一点是，因为 Anthropic 的性质，你知道，我们大约三年前才有了 API，对吧？那始于一个非常小的团队，团队增长得如此之快，系统如此迅速地承担了大量负载。在那段时间里，我们并没有完美的 Python 系统文档，我想这也是让整件事更具挑战性的原因之一。并不是说我们可以拿着这份文档照着做，然后构建一个新系统。所以从这个角度来看，我认为我们一直并且继续处于这样一个世界：代码本身在很大程度上就是为它工作的智能体的文档。但我觉得在系统设计以及所有这些部分如何组合在一起方面，看到新工程师加入时真的很有趣，他们会说，好吧，我得搞清楚这个系统，准备好上手工作。这部分变化很大，因为过去你会请人和你一起站在白板前，画出方框和箭头，了解发生了什么，也许还有一些图表可以研究、了解发生了什么。但现在我们看到人们加入后，他们做的就是直接问 Claude：告诉我这东西是怎么工作的。通常你会得到类似交互式应用的东西，不只是方框和箭头，而是真正的系统渲染，你可以点击浏览，说，好吧，这部分系统是这样与另一部分系统交互的。任何人都可以按自己喜欢的方式学习，对吧？比如他们想要这个可以深入点击的交互式应用，或者他们只想读文档来学习，对吧，或者他们想要视频风格或播客风格，对吧，你可以让 Claude 为你制作任何这些东西，来帮助你学习这个系统。这真是很酷的一点，每个人都用自己的方式来了解发生了什么。

turns.en: Yeah, this is kind of crazy but I guess the prerequisite is you have all the data connected. Like when you say Claude, it's not the same Claude as we use externally, but you have all your data sources, your code base, your observability, your post mortems, whatever, everything's there and then it can just search it, use it, do whatever it makes sense.
turns.zh: 是的，这有点疯狂，但我猜前提是你把所有数据都连接起来了。就像你说 Claude，它不是我们外部使用的那个 Claude，但你有所有的数据源、代码库、可观测性、事后复盘等等，一切都在那里，然后它就可以搜索、使用，做任何合理的事情。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. So the way that we work with Claude is very much like we have all of our systems have MCP servers and we have connections to those things, and Claude when we're working with it can just search through whatever it needs to to generate the right information that it needs for us.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。所以我们与 Claude 合作的方式非常像：我们所有的系统都有 MCP 服务器，我们与这些东西有连接，当我们与 Claude 合作时，它可以搜索它需要的任何东西，以生成它为我们所需的正确信息。

turns.en: This is still wild to me because I remember when I was at Uber, there's onboarding and engineers teach onboarding, and when it was my turn, I read some of the slides because they were outdated, to make them up to date on how these systems work. And then I was thinking to myself, okay, this is good. Every month or every two months we had a new onboarding session, and I kept teaching the same slides, and at some point they were kind of outdated, but I was like, nah, I can't be bothered to change it, so I was like, well, it's not exactly like this, but it's roughly like this, that's good enough. It's kind of strange to imagine now this reality that you can have a system that will always be up to date as long as the data is connected, and it can give you the formats that you like, interactive things. turns.zh: 这对我来说还是很不可思议，因为我记得我在 Uber 的时候，有入职培训，工程师来教入职培训。轮到我讲的时候，我读了一些幻灯片，因为它们过时了，我把它们更新到这些系统当前的工作方式。然后我心想，好吧，这挺好。每个月或每两个月我们都有新的入职培训，我一直在教同样的幻灯片，到某个时候它们有点过时了，但我想，算了，我懒得改，所以我就说，嗯，不完全是这样的，但大致是这样，够用了。现在想象这种现实，你可以有一个系统，只要数据连着，它就永远是最新的，还能给你喜欢的格式、交互式的东西，这有点奇怪。我以前从没听说过入职培训能这样，因为以前通常工作量太大、收益太小。

turns.en: Yeah, it's totally different now. And most of it, honestly, it's just the codebase itself.
turns.zh: 是啊，现在完全不一样了。而且说实话，大部分内容其实就是代码库本身。

turns.en: Yes, you can pull in data from, like you said earlier, postmortems and places like this, but for the most part, it's just like, look at the codebase. Claude does, look at the codebase, and then generate whatever you want.
turns.zh: 是的，你可以像你之前说的那样，从事故复盘之类的地方拉数据，但大部分时候，就是看代码库。Claude 会看代码库，然后生成你想要的任何东西。

ts.sec: Rewriting at Stripe and language choice

turns.en: So you've done similar style rewrites before AI at your other places. How different was this project, both in terms of timing and in terms of where the effort was spent, unexpected things, because now we're doing a completely different way of rewriting with AI. I'm sure there's a little bit of like mines that you find midway where like, oh, I wouldn't expect this. Like, okay, we need to fix this just because it's something new.
turns.zh: 所以你在 AI 之前，在其他公司做过类似风格的改写。这个项目有多不同，无论是时间上，还是精力花在哪里，以及意外的事情，因为现在我们用 AI 做完全不同的改写方式。我肯定你中途会遇到一些雷，比如，哦，我没想到这个。好吧，我们得修一下，因为这是新东西。

turns.en: Yeah. So at Stripe actually, we went through a, we were trying to build some V2 abstractions in Stripe's API. And one of the interesting things about this was there were some really deep debates on if we're going to build new services that are going to serve the V2 abstractions, do we write these in Ruby, which most of Stripe's codebase is Ruby, or do we choose a language that will have higher performance and better speed and these sorts of things? And at the time, it was Java that we were deciding between. And it's interesting because we actually went through a first period where a lot of code got written in Java as part of spinning up these new systems. And we ended up making a call part of the way through to just stop and say, this doesn't make any sense. We should build new services. We should build a clean system, but we should just do it in Ruby. The efficiencies that we were going to gain from doing so in Java didn't outweigh the fact that it was going to take us literally years to have all of this code get written. And so I think in that case it was understanding the language, the choices around those things, engineers putting hands on keyboard and writing code in a language they were unfamiliar with, all of that sort of stuff was just the things that now you can just gloss over and be like, yep, we don't have to think too hard about that. We'll all be okay because the model knows and it'll be fine. Whereas in the past that was just the biggest bottleneck and part of the thing that just took the longest is the learning and the implementation.
turns.zh: 是的。其实在 Stripe，我们经历了一个，我们试图在 Stripe 的 API 里构建一些 V2 抽象。有趣的一点是，当时有非常深入的辩论：如果我们要构建服务 V2 抽象的新服务，我们用 Ruby 写吗，Stripe 大部分代码库是 Ruby，还是选一门性能更高、速度更快的语言？当时我们在 Java 之间做选择。有趣的是，我们其实经历了第一阶段，很多代码用 Java 写，作为启动这些新系统的一部分。我们中途做了个决定，停下来，说这没道理。我们应该构建新服务，构建一个干净的系统，但就用 Ruby 做。用 Java 能获得的效率提升，抵不过我们要花好几年才能把所有代码写完这个事实。所以我觉得在那种情况下，理解语言、围绕这些的选择、工程师动手用不熟悉的语言写代码，所有这些现在都可以略过，说，对，我们不用太费心，大家都没问题，因为模型知道，会没事的。而过去，这恰恰是最大的瓶颈，也是最耗时的部分之一，就是学习和实现。

turns.en: Yeah, and I guess getting everyone to learn, like right, choosing a new language used to be that you either needed to train people. I say this hesitantly because one of my first two years when I worked at Uber, I think training was a bit of a curse where like, why would you train, like we all learned, we just picked it up, we had motivation. But then when we moved over, I think also Uber standardized languages was Java and Go, people were asking, like these engineers, could we just get some Java training, because I just want to know how to do some. A lot of coordination, everyone being enrolled, getting supported, things, and it just goes back to like even at the most, you know, the best engineers, at some point you want to make sure everyone's at the same level.
turns.zh: 是啊，我猜让所有人学习，对，选一门新语言过去要么需要培训人。我说这话有点犹豫，因为我在 Uber 的头两年，我觉得培训有点像诅咒，为什么要培训，我们都自己学，我们直接上手，我们有动力。但后来我们转过来，Uber 标准化语言是 Java 和 Go，人们在问，这些工程师，能不能给我们一些 Java 培训，因为我就是想知道怎么做一些。很多协调，每个人报名，得到支持，等等，这就回到，即使是最优秀的工程师，某个时候你也想确保每个人都在同一水平。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: Sounds like kind of like AI gives us a bit of this equalizer like well if you need training you have your trainer if you do.
turns.zh: 听起来 AI 给了我们一点这种均衡器，如果你需要培训，你有你的培训师，如果你需要的话。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And you just like skip that whole part. Funny enough actually when I was at Betterment we did a, everything was Java and then we decided to build the user facing application layer in Ruby. And at the time we did a very similar, it was Ruby on Rails. We did the similar, you go through all the Michael Hartl tutorials and all those sorts of things and you spend hours and hours and hours with engineers learning the language and you decide for yourself like that's an investment worth making because you get to the other side of that everybody knows what they're doing and then you can get this work done. But first it was like that is easier to stomach because the model will help write code and it'll help you learn and all those sorts of things. But then you get all the way to the point where it's like it really truly doesn't matter if the engineers like can understand every last teeny piece of syntax and so you just don't have to think about the investment that you would have to make up front on learning.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。你就跳过那整部分。有趣的是，我在 Betterment 的时候，我们做了一切都是 Java，然后我们决定用 Ruby 构建面向用户的应用层。当时我们做了非常类似的，是 Ruby on Rails。我们做了类似的，你过一遍所有 Michael Hartl 教程之类的，你花几个小时几个小时和工程师学语言，你自己决定这是值得的投资，因为过了那一关，每个人都知道自己在做什么，然后你可以完成工作。但首先，那更容易接受，因为模型会帮忙写代码，会帮你学习之类的。但然后你一路走到那个点，工程师是否能理解每一个微小的语法细节，真的不重要了，所以你就不用考虑前期在学习上必须做的投资。

turns.zh: 可以这么说吗，作为工程师，具体语言并不真的重要，我知道和理解每门具体语言，我是说一旦我懂了概念？

turns.zh: 是的，到这个时候真的开始不重要了。

turns.zh: 作为工程师说这话不心痛吗？我是说我和你，学一门语言花了很长时间和精力，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah, but I think it's interesting. I think everyone feels differently, probably, on this front. I think when we first started to have tab complete, right? And tools like that. Yeah, exactly. And that felt great, right? Because you were like, I don't need to type these last few, you know? And so, I think from that perspective, it depends if you're the kind of engineer who cares about these things because of the end result of the thing that you're building and you're just excited to create something and build. If you're the kind of engineer who really did deeply enjoy the nitty-gritty of languages and these sorts of things, for what it's worth, I think there's still plenty of work for people who do care about that sort of thing, like deep work on evolving what should the next languages be or how do we make these frameworks more efficient over time.
turns.zh: 是的，但我觉得这很有趣。我觉得每个人在这方面的感受可能都不一样。我觉得当我们刚开始有 Tab 补全的时候，对吧？还有类似的工具。对，没错。那感觉很好，对吧？因为你会觉得，我不需要打最后这几个字了，你知道吗？所以，从那个角度看，这取决于你是哪种工程师。如果你是因为你构建的东西的最终结果而在意这些，你只是兴奋于创造和构建，那你可以快得多，也可以雄心大得多，那感觉很好。如果你是那种真的深深享受语言细节之类东西的工程师，我想说，在意这些的人仍然有很多工作，比如深度工作，演进下一门语言应该是什么，或者我们如何让这些框架随着时间更高效。

turns.en: But I think for the average engineer, you might feel sad if you did enjoy those sorts of things, but I think for a lot of people, the people who were happy when they got to start tab completing, you probably aren't too sad because you're more focused on what you're able to create now.
turns.zh: 但我觉得对普通工程师来说，如果你确实喜欢那些东西，你可能会感到难过，但我认为对很多人来说，那些开始用上 tab 补全时感到高兴的人，你可能不会太难过，因为你更关注你现在能创造什么。

turns.en: I also wonder for the engineers who are really invested in the craft and in the what and the how it works. Again, I just wonder if maybe we never had that conversation of like, all right, like on a hobby project or on your side project, it's great, right? And I think there will be people who will write code because you enjoy it, because you do it. But if you're building at a business, there's a question of like, why are you here? turns.zh: 我也在想，对于那些真正投入于工艺、投入于做什么以及如何运作的工程师来说。我只是在想，也许我们从未有过那样的对话，比如，好吧，在业余项目或你的副业项目上，那很棒，对吧？我认为会有人因为享受而写代码，因为你喜欢做这件事。但如果你是在为企业开发，问题就是，你为什么在这里？我真不愿这么说，但没有企业会雇佣工程师来写漂亮的代码，除非他们是在卖某种关于漂亮代码的东西。但它总是为了一个目标。

turns.zh: 是的。

turns.zh: 而追求漂亮代码的原因通常是可维护性，为了更容易、为了更好的性能、更好的非功能性需求。如果你能用另一种方式做到，那是一种务实的态度，说，好吧，我的意思是，让我关注更大的图景，也就是用我能用的最好的工具来帮助实现这个目标。

turns.zh: 是的，没错。所以，你知道，就像你说的，我认为对于那些深深关心这类事情的人，如果你从事语言本身的工作，仍然有工作可做，对吧？如果你在这些领域工作，你大概应该去做那个，如果你真的深深关心那些东西，因为如果你关心那些事情，你可以做很多很酷的雄心勃勃的工作。但如果你在一个企业里工作，语言和框架的选择都只是实现某个目标的手段，也就是创造能赚钱或完成企业使命的东西，那么很难让一个人如此深入地花时间在那些事情上，而这种方式最终对实现目标和创造结果并不重要。

How quickly was this completed-ish?
turns.zh: 现在，基于这一个项目，这次重写，看起来 AI 承担了很多繁重的工作。它把一个老实说可能需要数年才能完成的项目——我们知道这些迁移有多复杂，甚至可能中途被回滚——变成了只是把它完成。这大概有多快完成？

And that's kind of keeping in mind that there was some upfront time where one or two people were like, we might want to do this, right? And did a little investigation before we actually had people go and work on it. But yeah, I want to say it was something like five or six months, and the core team was relatively small that was doing this. But that team had to then
turns.zh: 是的，所以我想说大概五到六个月左右。这还要考虑到有一些前期时间，有一两个人说，我们可能想做这个，对吧？在我们实际派人去做之前做了一些调查。但是的，我想说大概五到六个月，做这个的核心团队相对较小。但那个团队然后必须

turns.en: A few people.
turns.zh: 几个人。

turns.en: Yeah, something like that. But then I think that team had to go and work with people on a bunch of other teams, right? Who owned the various parts of the system. And I think one of the things that was most complex that was happening was all those other teams were still doing work, right? Like we didn't stop developing the Python system when all of this was happening. And so at first it was kind of like, okay, fine, we're just trying to get the very basic core of what we kind of call the token hot path done. And these things around the edges that are new that are getting worked on, whatever, we'll kind of come back to those later. But then we had at least one instance where a beta kind of went to GA on the Python system when the rest team wasn't expecting it, and all of a sudden that shadow traffic system was showing a lot of differences, a lot of errors. They were like, what's going on? Oh, okay, new feature went GA. And from there they added just like linting and static analysis sort of thing, so that if any other team around them was working on a new feature, they couldn't just build the Python part. They had to also do the Rust implementation because at a certain point we were close enough, right? Like you kind of have to be in a world where you can't just have people randomly flipping on new features on the Python side and then the Rust team is trying to catch up. You have to get to a place where all the teams around them were building in both. And then we wanted to minimize that period of time and as quickly as possible get to a place where we could shut down the Python systems so that you don't have all of those teams needing to think about both sides.
turns.zh: 是的，差不多。但后来我觉得那个团队必须去和其他许多团队的人合作，对吧？那些团队拥有系统的各个部分。我认为发生的最复杂的事情之一是所有那些其他团队仍在工作，对吧？就像在整个过程中我们没有停止开发 Python 系统。所以一开始有点像，好吧，我们只是试图完成我们称之为 token 热路径的最基本核心。而那些边缘的新东西正在被处理，不管怎样，我们以后再回来处理那些。但后来我们至少有一个实例，一个 beta 在 Python 系统上转为 GA，而 rest 团队没有预料到，突然那个影子流量系统显示出很多差异，很多错误。他们说，怎么了？哦，好吧，新功能转为 GA 了。从那时起，他们添加了类似 linting 和静态分析的东西，这样如果周围的任何其他团队正在开发新功能，他们不能只构建 Python 部分。他们还必须做 Rust 实现，因为在某个时候我们已经足够接近了，对吧？你有点必须进入一个世界，你不能只是让人随机在 Python 侧开启新功能，然后 Rust 团队试图追赶。你必须达到一个所有周围团队都在两边构建的状态。然后我们想最小化那段时间，尽快达到可以关闭 Python 系统的状态，这样你就不需要所有那些团队都考虑两边。

turns.en: What I'm picking up is the bulk of the work that engineers spend their time was not like writing the code because you had the agents do it and you coordinated them and had them tested, but it was coordinating with other teams, what are you working on? We're going to be doing this. Is it impacting your work? Or when something is investigating, when something is not going like that.
turns.zh: 我理解的是，工程师花费大部分时间的工作不是写代码，因为你让智能体去做，你协调它们并让它们测试，而是与其他团队协调，你在做什么？我们将要做这个。它是否影响你的工作？或者当某件事在调查时，当某件事进展不顺利时。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So it sounds like there's still a lot of work involved. You see what I mean? Even though there's a lot of heavy lifting has been done by Claude.
turns.zh: 所以听起来仍然涉及很多工作。你明白我的意思吗？即使 Claude 已经完成了大量繁重的工作。

turns.en: We mean and we think about that with everything we do. I think the average engineer is spending so much more of their time on that type of coordination work and much less on actual implementation. And even like orchestrating agents. I think some of this to some extent is like you've got to go tell your agents like get something done for me, right? But even from there agents are often orchestrating other agents and the humans not necessarily spending a ton of time on that. It's much more so the other teams, the other people and how do we make sure that all these pieces are going to come together, that people are on the same page, people are spending so much more of their time on that sort of thing than on the work of actually getting the thing built.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我们做每件事时都会考虑这一点。我认为普通工程师花在那类协调工作上的时间多得多，而花在实际实现上的时间少得多。甚至像编排智能体。我认为其中一些在某种程度上就像你必须去告诉你的智能体，帮我完成某件事，对吧？但即使从那里开始，智能体经常在编排其他智能体，而人类不一定花大量时间在那上面。更多的是其他团队、其他人，以及我们如何确保所有这些部分能结合在一起，人们达成共识，人们花在那类事情上的时间比实际构建东西的工作多得多。

turns.en: So this was a migration. But can we talk about a Claude Managed Agents project where you built something brand new? I think we talked about Claude Managed Agents which is also a very ambitious project. How did building that happen especially when you compare it with how it would have happened in the past?
turns.zh: 所以这是一次迁移。但我们可以谈谈一个 Claude Managed Agents 项目，你们构建了全新的东西吗？我想我们谈过 Claude Managed Agents，这也是一个非常雄心勃勃的项目。构建那个项目是如何发生的，特别是当你与过去会如何发生相比？

turns.en: Yeah. So Claude Managed Agents just as you map for a second. So the Claude platform, when I first started a year ago, a little over a year ago, was just the messages API, just this like stateless API. And then models were getting better and better at running for longer and you know, of course people said, okay, great, we're going to move agents to mostly run in the cloud and enable them to eventually run more autonomously.
turns.zh: 是的。所以 Claude Managed Agents，就像你稍微映射一下。所以 Claude 平台，当我一年前、一年多前刚开始时，只是 messages API，只是这个无状态 API。然后模型在运行更长时间方面变得越来越好，你知道，当然人们说，好吧，太好了，我们将把智能体主要移到云端运行，并使它们最终能更自主地运行。

turns.en: And so people were building harnesses and they were deploying those harnesses to the cloud. And everyone was running into some of the same types of issues when you do that, which is, you know, from a reliability perspective, if you run these agents inside of a sandbox and your sandbox dies and your agent dies, right? Or security, right? Like if you have your agent running in the sandbox and do the credentials go in the sandbox with the agent, right? There's a lot of problems that you run into when you think about these cloud-based agents and their architecture. And so we ended up building a whole new suite of APIs within the cloud platform that were just kind of higher order and meant for the ability to define an agent and then start a session and run that agent. And so as part of doing this, that meant we were building services that could run the harness, could store the session state, could handle spawning sandboxes as needed and all of these sorts of different things. And it was interesting for this set of services we chose Go. And this was in part because this was first of all just before we had done the Rust migration and we were still in that period where we wanted to pick a language that would allow us to build efficient services and these sorts of things, but still have pretty good developer experience for the humans who were looking at the code. And I think for this, it was much, much, much more so all of the work on defining the API abstractions and thinking about the service architecture and the service diagrams and solving for some of these problems like reliability and security and latency and way less on implementation and actually building, you know, like writing the code that would power each of these individual services. So from that perspective, that one too just so different than in the past where you'd spend a whole bunch of time planning and then a whole bunch of time implementing, you really, really, really shrink the implementation part and then you get quicker to verification and making sure that everything works well and is that high quality before you go and launch it publicly.
turns.zh: 于是人们开始构建 harness，并将这些 harness 部署到云端。每个人在这样做时都会遇到一些相同类型的问题，比如从可靠性的角度来看，如果你在沙箱中运行这些智能体，而沙箱挂了，你的智能体也就挂了，对吧？或者安全性问题，如果你的智能体在沙箱中运行，凭证是否也要放在沙箱里和智能体在一起？当你考虑这些基于云的智能体及其架构时，会遇到很多问题。因此，我们最终在云平台内构建了一套全新的 API，这些 API 层次更高，旨在能够定义智能体，然后启动会话并运行该智能体。在实现这一点的过程中，这意味着我们要构建能够运行 harness、存储会话状态、按需生成沙箱以及处理所有这些不同事项的服务。有趣的是，对于这组服务，我们选择了 Go 语言。部分原因是，首先，这发生在我们进行 Rust 迁移之前，我们仍处于那个时期：我们希望选择一种能让我们构建高效服务等功能的语言，同时对于查看代码的人来说仍有相当好的开发者体验。我认为对于这个项目，更多得多的工作在于定义 API 抽象、思考服务架构和服务图，以及解决可靠性、安全性和延迟等问题，而实现和实际构建——即编写驱动每个单独服务的代码——所占比重小得多。所以从这个角度来看，那个项目也与过去大不相同：过去你会花大量时间做规划，然后花大量时间实现；现在你大大缩短了实现部分，然后更快地进入验证阶段，确保一切正常工作且质量高，然后再公开发布。

turns.en: Oh, yeah yeah yeah. So okay. turns.zh: 哦，对对对。好的。那么对于托管智能体，我们开始的地方，我们做的第一件事是，我们说，好吧，我们要构建这个系统来运行云智能体，我们既希望让 API 客户能够构建智能体，也希望让Claude Code团队能够实现网页和移动体验，这样你就不必只是——你知道，Claude Code CLI 只是运行在你的笔记本电脑上，或者桌面应用运行在你的笔记本电脑上，但我们希望让人们能够发起在云端运行的Claude Code会话，你可以走开，稍后再回来。而且因为把这种智能体架构做对非常复杂，我们想我们可以共享这部分，对吧？比如我们构建这个架构，它可以同时支持两者。有趣的是，我们做的第一件事，最明显的起点是，很好，一个 API 请求进来，你生成一个沙箱，并在该沙箱内启动Claude Code，然后你就有了一个智能体。

turns.en: Then you're you have to start from scratch.

turns.en: Yeah. The second was latency. We like really didn't like this idea that if you boot Claude Code inside of the sandbox, then whenever you do want to go call tools and external services, you end up needing to have credentials inside that sandbox with the agents that has access to the model, right? And so that wasn't good. And then lastly, um hilariously, CPU was a thing. So we're booting and running a sandbox for every single one of these uh
turns.zh: 是的。第二个是延迟。为了真正获得任何 token 返回，你必须等待沙箱启动，然后等待Claude Code在沙箱内启动，然后才能与模型对话并流式返回这些 token。所以那是个问题。第三个是安全性。我们真的很不喜欢这个想法：如果你在沙箱内启动Claude Code，那么每当你想要调用工具和外部服务时，你最终需要在那个沙箱内拥有凭证，而智能体可以访问模型，对吧？所以那不好。最后，嗯，好笑的是，CPU 也是个问题。所以我们要为每一个这样的……启动并运行一个沙箱。

turns.en: Every one of these is at one CPU or more.
turns.zh: 每一个都至少占用一个 CPU 或更多。

turns.en: Right. So we had these four problems, and we first actually, we launched the Claude Code web experience in like an early beta, and we launched the API in early beta. And we just like weren't happy with any of these problems, and we were kind of trying to scramble to do all the things to like individually solve each of these problems. But again, just speaking of things that are possible now that weren't super possible earlier, we ended up going back to the drawing board a bit and saying, what if we from first principles like redesigned and rearchitected this thing instead of just doing the like easy thing that works, which is, you know, boot a box and boot Claude Code inside of it? What if we designed this from first principles? And what we ended up with was you would run your harness on a durable server, and you would only spawn sandboxes to execute work as needed. And then you'd have your separate session storage. And in that world, you solve for reliability because your harness is on a durable server, and if any of those sandboxes die, your agent is fine. You solve for latency because the request comes in to that durable server, and it goes basically straight through to the messages API, and so it's like the teeniest bit of latency on top of the messages API. So that was great. Security was solved because the way that we ended up doing this was if you have an agent choosing to call an external system to call a tool in an MCP server or, you know, go out over the internet, we can just kind of run a proxy along the side and keep all of our credentials separately in a vault. And then when you do go to make that request, you can inject the credential at egress just in time on the way out so that that credential never needs to be inside of the sandbox. And then CPU was great because we found ourselves running on average around a third of the CPU for this system as the original system. And so we threw the whole thing out and we rebuilt it before we went that way.
turns.zh: 对。所以我们有这四个问题，我们最初实际上推出了Claude Code网页体验的早期测试版，也推出了 API 的早期测试版。我们只是对这些问题的任何一个都不满意，我们有点在拼命地做所有事情来单独解决每个问题。但再次说到现在可能而以前不太可能的事情，我们最终有点回到绘图板，说，如果我们从第一性原理重新设计和重新架构这个东西，而不是只做简单的可行方案——也就是启动一个盒子并在里面启动Claude Code——会怎样？如果我们从第一性原理设计会怎样？我们最终得到的是，你会在一个持久服务器上运行你的 harness，并且只在需要执行工作时才生成沙箱。然后你有单独的会话存储。在那个世界里，你解决了可靠性问题，因为你的 harness 在持久服务器上，如果那些沙箱中的任何一个挂了，你的智能体没事。你解决了延迟问题，因为请求到达那个持久服务器，它基本上直接传到消息 API，所以在消息 API 之上只有极小的延迟。所以那很好。安全性也解决了，因为我们最终做的方式是，如果你有一个智能体选择调用外部系统来调用 MCP 服务器中的工具，或者你知道，通过互联网出去，我们可以直接在旁边运行一个代理，并将所有凭证单独保存在一个保险库中。然后当你确实要发出请求时，你可以在出口处及时注入凭证，这样凭证就永远不需要在沙箱内部。然后 CPU 也很好，因为我们发现这个系统平均只运行原始系统大约三分之一的 CPU。所以我们在采用那条路之前，把整个东西扔掉了并重建了它。
