ts.sec: How Anthropic Uses Claude in Slack

turns.en: I think people probably picture Anthropic Slack as having all these crazy agents that all have their own identities and everything, right? And it's not really quite how we work. We're much more like — and we designed Claude Tag after this concept — it's like you've got Claude and you work with Claude. And it maybe has different permissions and works a little bit differently in different contexts, in a DM or a channel or whatever it might be, but for the most part this concept kind of stays the same. So that's really the biggest one: you're mostly in Slack and you're interacting with Claude alongside humans in anything that you're working on.
turns.zh: 我想大家大概会想象 Anthropic 的 Slack 里全是各种疯狂的智能体，每个都有自己的身份之类的，对吧？其实我们并不是那样工作的。我们更像是——Claude Tag 就是按这个理念设计的——你有一个 Claude，你和 Claude 一起工作。它在不同场景下可能有不同的权限、表现得略有不同，比如在私信里、在频道里或别的什么地方，但大体上这个理念是不变的。所以最重要的一点就是：你大部分时间都在 Slack 里，无论做什么，你都是和人类一起与 Claude 互动。

turns.en: So once I'm onboarded, or in the company as an engineer, and I start to contribute and build stuff — like back pre-AI, the way it would have looked is I do some sort of planning, I align with someone on my team, I write the code, I create a pull request, I go through code review, CI/CD runs, I get sign-off, I get feedback from my teammates, I fix them, I deploy, there are ways that I can monitor. I might actually even do a feature flag when it's a large system. And then there's monitoring, alerting, and I'm on call, and if an incident happens I do a postmortem. That's kind of a typical thing that an engineer will do in their first month once they're fully there. How has this changed? Because I know — we know — writing code itself has changed. I no longer write it. But what is left of the old-school tools that we use, and what has just been taken over by agents? How have the workflows changed inside?
turns.zh: 那么，一旦我入职了，或者作为工程师进入公司，开始贡献、开始构建东西——在 AI 之前，流程大概是这样：我做些规划，和团队里的某个人对齐，写代码，创建 pull request，走代码审查，CI/CD 跑起来，拿到签字确认，收到队友的反馈，我修好问题，部署上线，还有各种监控手段。系统大的时候我甚至可能加个功能开关。然后是监控、告警，我还要值班，出了事故就做复盘。这大概是一个工程师完全到位后第一个月会做的典型事情。这一切是怎么变化的？因为我知道——我们都知道——写代码本身已经变了。我不再自己写了。但那些老派的工具还剩下什么？哪些已经被智能体接管了？内部的工作流到底怎么变了？

turns.en: So I would say the way we kind of think about it is less on the life cycle of an individual change and individual pull request that you might think about, and more just the overall project or just some higher unit of work that you might be thinking about, because you're working with agents and to some extent these agents are directly orchestrated by you, right? To say I'm going to pick up this Linear task and I'm going to get this exact small thing done, and that's going to lead to one pull request and that thing is going to get merged. But much more so, you're kind of zooming up a layer and thinking about: I want to accomplish something that requires end-to-end building of all these different components, right? And so you'll probably ideate a little bit with Claude, and just kind of go back and forth and plan and think about how you might want to get something done. And then you send Claude off to go and do this work.
turns.zh: 我会说，我们的思路不太放在单个改动、单个 pull request 的生命周期上，而更多是放在整个项目，或者你正在考虑的一个更高层级的工作单元上，因为你在和智能体协作，而这些智能体在某种程度上是由你直接编排的，对吧？比如我说我要接这个 Linear 任务，把这个具体的小事做完，这会产出一个 pull request，然后它会被合并。但更多时候，你是往上跳了一层，去想：我要完成一件事，而这件事需要端到端地构建所有这些不同的组件，对吧？所以你可能会先和 Claude 一起头脑风暴一下，来回讨论，做规划，想想怎么把这件事做成。然后你就把 Claude 派出去做这个工作。

turns.en: But I think what's interesting about this is that in that kind of development loop, there are a lot of aspects that maybe you aren't really even in the loop on anymore that you would have been previously. So a good example is there are certain types of pull requests that can get opened that don't really even need you to look at it, or somebody else to look at it. And we're doing a lot of work on getting to a place where we get more and more comfortable with more of these types of changes not requiring a human in the loop, because you can picture the types of changes that are maybe just so mechanical, right? A good example is we release new versions of our SDKs whenever we have a new API version or a new model. There are aspects of our SDKs — just doing the version bump in those SDKs — that you don't really need a human to be spending tons of time on, because the code change that needs to happen is very mechanical, and getting that reviewed and all the way through is pretty mechanical.
turns.zh: 但我觉得有意思的是，在这种开发循环里，有很多环节你可能已经不在环内了，而以前你是在的。举个例子，有些类型的 pull request 被开出来之后，其实根本不需要你去看，也不需要别人去看。我们正在做很多工作，朝着一个越来越适应这类改动、不再需要人类在环内的方向走，因为你可以想象，有些改动就是非常机械的，对吧？一个很好的例子是：每当我们有新版本的 API 或新模型，就会发布新版本的 SDK。SDK 里有些部分——比如只是把版本号往上提——你真的不需要人类花大量时间在这上面，因为需要发生的代码改动非常机械，把它审查完、走完流程也相当机械。

turns.en: And so we've taken changes like that and done everything that we can to say Claude will go and open the pull request. Then we've got a Claude that reviews it first and decides: is this actually fitting into one of these mechanical changes we know how to do, or is it a riskier change that should be human?
turns.zh: 所以我们就把这类改动拿过来，尽一切努力让 Claude 去开 pull request。然后我们有一个 Claude 先来审查，判断：这到底属于我们已知如何处理的机械改动，还是一个风险更高、应该由人类来看的改动？

turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，正是这样。

turns.en: Exactly. And either a human does have to look at it or not. And if not, then it can go and get merged and get deployed without a human needing to be in the loop. And I think going back to your original question — I'm a new engineer and there's this whole change lifecycle that happens — there are just a lot of pieces of getting something done end to end that you might not have to think about. Of all the PRs that went into something getting done, you might have interacted with and been a part of some subset of them, and then there are some where agents are running and doing their thing and you're not really a part of what's happening there.
turns.zh: 正是如此。要么确实需要人类来看，要么不需要。如果不需要，它就可以被合并、被部署，全程不需要人类在环内。回到你最初的问题——我是一个新工程师，有整套改动生命周期在运转——把一件事端到端做完，有很多环节你可能根本不用去想。在促成某件事完成的所有 PR 里，你可能只参与并接触了其中一部分，还有一些是智能体在跑、在做它们的事，你并不真正参与其中。

turns.en: And I think that's the big shift that everybody is seeing: the difference between I'm a human and I'm working with an agent either directly on my laptop or I'm orchestrating it in the cloud or whatever, versus agents that are persistent and taking actions like classifying a change and reviewing that change. Or like we have agents running that, when CI goes red — a flaky test was merged into main — sure, somebody can go and say oh, CI's red, I've got to fix that test, but now we just have agents running that will go and do that for you and nobody really has to look, right? So there are just more aspects of the process that are totally human out of the loop now, which I think is just something for everybody to wrap their heads around.
turns.zh: 我觉得这就是大家看到的最大转变：一边是我作为人类，直接在自己的笔记本上和智能体协作，或者在云端编排它之类的；另一边是持久运行的智能体在采取行动，比如给改动分类、审查改动。又比如我们有一些智能体在跑：当 CI 变红——一个不稳定的测试被合进了 main——当然，可以有人跑过去说“哦 CI 红了，我得去修那个测试”，但现在我们就是有智能体在跑，会替你做这件事，根本没人需要去看，对吧？所以流程中越来越多的环节现在完全把人类排除在环外了，我觉得这是大家需要慢慢消化的一件事。

turns.en: So but just specifically — because I know this will make so much sense when you're inside Anthropic, but from the outside — okay, so I now have a project or a feature I want to build. I decide it's a good idea, or I believe it's a good idea. I'll chat with Claude, make a plan. I'll probably spin off a couple of agents to start to build it. One of them does scaffolding, the other one builds it, the other one does, I don't know, validation, or maybe another feature, etc. They go off, and then what do I see next? Is there a place where I'll be pinged when they're ready for a review? They're still a team, so I'm inside a team. Do I decide — do I pull another human in and say can you look at this as well? So what happens after this point, after the agents build that stuff?
turns.zh: 但具体来说——因为我知道在 Anthropic 内部这会非常顺理成章，但从外部看——好，我现在有一个想做的项目或功能。我判断这是个好主意，或者我相信这是个好主意。我会和 Claude 聊，做个计划。我大概会派出几个智能体开始构建。一个做脚手架，另一个负责实现，再一个做，我也不知道，验证，或者做另一个功能，等等。它们跑出去了，然后我接下来看到什么？有没有一个地方，在它们准备好接受审查时会通知我？它们仍然是一个团队，而我在一个团队里。是我来决定——是我拉另一个人进来说“你能也看看这个吗”？所以在这个节点之后，智能体把这些东西建好之后，会发生什么？

turns.en: So your agents are typically — and maybe the main point that I'm making is — you're sending those first agents off, and those agents are probably spawning other tasks that you aren't necessarily even choosing to orchestrate yourself, right? On the path to this bigger goal that's happening. The way that we work with our agents in Slack is they're pretty chatty. And so they'll very often come back and be like, okay, great, I've got this pull request up.
turns.zh: 你的智能体通常会——也许我想说的重点是——你把第一批智能体派出去，而那些智能体很可能又在派生其他任务，这些任务甚至不一定是你自己选择去编排的，对吧？在通往那个更大目标的路上。我们在 Slack 里和智能体协作的方式是，它们话挺多的。所以它们经常会回来跟你说：好，很棒，我把这个 pull request 开好了。

turns.en: So you're kind of saying that the agents, when they go off—so for example, I might be building a feature on this specific system, and I tell the agent, 'All right, here's my goal. This is what I want to do. Here's the first sub-task we're going to do.' And then the agent goes off and it might say, 'Oh, by the way, I checked some analytics. Here's an interesting thing. Here's something important that I think we should do. I'm suggesting we build this feature.' And then that's what you're saying—that they might come back being chatty, and then you can make a decision or steer it, basically, right?
turns.zh: 所以你的意思是，当智能体开始执行任务时——比如，我可能正在某个特定系统上构建一个功能，我告诉智能体：“好的，这是我的目标。这是我想做的事情。这是我们要做的第一个子任务。”然后智能体开始工作，它可能会说：“哦，顺便说一下，我查看了一些分析数据。这里有个有趣的事情。我认为我们应该做这件重要的事情。我建议我们构建这个功能。”然后这就是你说的——它们可能会回来跟你聊天，然后你可以做决定或者引导它，基本上是这样，对吧？

turns.en: Right. And it might say, 'Oh, you know, this other team has this piece of code that's kind of related, and maybe they're doing something that we don't understand yet, and we should ping them. Do you want me to ping them for you?' Right?
turns.zh: 对。它可能会说：“哦，你知道，另一个团队有这段相关的代码，也许他们正在做一些我们还不理解的事情，我们应该联系他们。你想让我帮你联系他们吗？”对吧？

turns.en: I get it. I get it. So it will be very interactive based on what you said—you can either pay attention to it or you can just kind of let it go, like, 'I go on.'
turns.zh: 我明白了。我明白了。所以根据你说的，它会非常互动——你可以选择关注它，或者就随它去，比如“我继续”。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And I think if it really needs your attention or else it's going to get stuck, it'll get your attention, right? But I think a lot of what we're trying to do is make more and more of this something that doesn't require you to have to get involved and be like—you know, it wouldn't be a great job if all he did was sit there and watch a Slack thread and then say yes or no or 'Okay, fine, I'll go ping that person,' right? That just wouldn't be interesting.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我认为如果它真的需要你的关注，否则就会卡住，它就会引起你的注意，对吧？但我认为我们正在努力做的很多事情是让越来越多的这类工作不需要你参与，就像——你知道，如果它只是坐在那里看 Slack 线程，然后说 yes 或 no 或者“好吧，我去联系那个人”，那可不是一份好工作，对吧？那根本不会有趣。

turns.en: I wanted to ask you about code review in the sense that pre-AI, a place like Stripe that I also worked at, you always had mandatory code reviews from another human, another engineer, for many reasons. A lot of it was not even related to that, but they were mandatory. Do you have that, or do you just say, 'I will give trust and accountability to the engineer who's building it, and they will decide: do I need to pull in someone, or does this look good because I verified it, or I know it's not a big deal?'
turns.zh: 我想问问关于代码审查的事情，因为在 AI 之前，像 Stripe 这样的地方——我也在那里工作过——你总是有来自另一个人类、另一个工程师的强制代码审查，原因很多。很多甚至与此无关，但它们是强制性的。你们有这种制度吗，还是说你们只是说：“我会把信任和责任交给构建它的工程师，他们会决定：我需要拉人进来吗，或者这看起来不错，因为我已经验证过了，或者我知道这没什么大不了的？”

turns.en: Yeah, so we have a system that—it's a cloud, but it's a classifier. But it runs on every change, and it decides: does this need a human look? If so, how many humans and what teams does it need? Or is this something that can merge directly without a human looking at it? And this is where I mentioned this idea of a very mechanical change. We're trying to do this thing where you define: what are the changes that end-to-end you shouldn't have to spend time on? We've done these things a million times. They all look the same. So can we classify this change as one of those very mechanical ones, like getting a new SDK version released? And if so, and it fits that mold, then okay, great. Claude's job is to make sure: is this thing going to have the outcome that is intended by the original change? And if so, great—a human doesn't have to look at it. But if it's like, eh, this might have some unintended side effects, or this is a little bit of a riskier change, or it's just a change happening in a system where we're not yet comfortable with zero humans paying any attention, then it will ping for a human to take a look. But we have pretty strong goals on getting to more and more of these changes where the classifier ends up deciding, 'No, I don't need a human to look at this at all.' And right now, we've got a small number of these things happening and it's ratcheting up. But for risky changes, we definitely still have humans looking at these.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我们有一个系统——它是个云，但也是个分类器。它会在每次变更时运行，并决定：这需要人工查看吗？如果需要，需要多少人和哪些团队？或者这是可以直接合并而无需人工查看的吗？这就是我提到的非常机械的变更的想法。我们试图做的是：你定义哪些变更端到端你不应该花时间在上面？我们已经做过这些事一百万次了。它们看起来都一样。那么，我们能否将这次变更归类为那些非常机械的变更之一，比如发布新的 SDK 版本？如果是，并且符合那个模式，那么好的，很好。Claude 的工作是确保：这件事会产生原始变更所预期的结果吗？如果是，很好——人类不必查看它。但如果它像是，呃，这可能会有一些意外的副作用，或者这是一个风险稍高的变更，或者它只是发生在一个我们还不放心让零个人关注的系统中的变更，那么它就会通知人类来查看。但我们有非常强烈的目标，要让越来越多的这类变更最终由分类器决定：“不，我根本不需要人类查看这个。”现在，我们已经有少量这样的变更在发生，而且正在逐步增加。但对于有风险的变更，我们肯定仍然有人类在查看。

turns.en: Once it gets deployed through different change gates, in production monitoring and incident management, how do you do that? Because again, pre-AI, you would have your dashboards that you would define, you would manually put together alerts on how you do it. Or, and of course, in more advanced places like Stripe and Uber, you would have machine learning systems already—this is like even 10 years ago—that would look at the signals and flag, 'Oh, something is wrong. Let's raise an alert.' A human gets paged whenever that time is. That person looks into it, and then later we go back. If it was false, they would try to tweak the alert. The on-call part would be also very heavy typically on high-impact systems as well. And of course, your system, the APIs, has as high impact as it goes. If it sneezes, a lot of people are relying on it to notice. How do you go about this kind of monitoring and on-call management, and how is Claude helping there?
turns.zh: 一旦它通过不同的变更门部署，在生产监控和事件管理方面，你们怎么做？因为同样，在 AI 之前，你会有你定义的仪表板，你会手动设置警报。或者，当然，在像 Stripe 和 Uber 这样更先进的地方，你已经有机器学习系统——甚至 10 年前——会查看信号并标记：“哦，出问题了。让我们发出警报。”人类会在任何时候被呼叫。那个人会调查，然后后来我们回去。如果是误报，他们会尝试调整警报。待命部分通常在高影响系统上也非常繁重。当然，你们的系统，API，影响非常大。如果它打个喷嚏，很多人依赖它来注意到。你们如何进行这种监控和待命管理，Claude 在那里如何帮助？

turns.en: Yeah. So a lot of it is really similar. A lot of it is, you know, we have all of our monitors and our detectors and our alerts that fire, and just like any other engineering team, often we get noise, right? Like you get alerted about something that's not really an issue.
turns.zh: 是的。所以很多方面真的很相似。很多是，你知道，我们有所有的监控器、检测器和警报会触发，就像任何其他工程团队一样，我们经常遇到噪音，对吧？比如你收到关于某些不是真正问题的警报。

turns.en: That's just how it is.
turns.zh: 就是这样。

turns.en: Yeah. So what we've started to do with our API on-call rotation, which is a very load-bearing on-call rotation, we've had happening over the past many months is we've had a Claude shadowing our on-call.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我们开始对我们的 API 待命轮换——这是一个非常关键的待命轮换——过去几个月我们让 Claude 影子跟随我们的待命人员。

turns.en: Oh, interesting.
turns.zh: 哦，有趣。

turns.en: Yeah. And the goal is to get to a point where when a page comes in—and we're just starting to do this—when a page comes in, it goes to that Claude first.
turns.zh: 是的。目标是达到这样一个点：当有页面进来时——我们刚刚开始这样做——当页面进来时，它首先发给那个 Claude。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And that Claude can decide: is this noise or is this real? And that's just the first gate. The first gate is: is it noise or is it real? And if it's noise, then really what we're trying to do is avoid a human getting interrupted or woken up or whatever it might be. And so we've started to do this and we've saved a lot in terms of human time that would have gone to looking into something that turned out to be noise. And then when it goes and says, 'Okay, this is real,' in which case it escalates the page to a human and the human will come in and start to look. But in that time when we're waiting for a human to come in and start to look, the Claude will start to also look and figure out what might I be able to do to fix this problem. And often by the time a human—especially if it's the middle of the night and somebody's getting woken up—by the time they get to their laptop, Claude has diagnosed the issue and has a recommended fix, and maybe it's even started to take some action towards that fix that a human just needs to be like, 'Yes, thank you, that sounds great.' And of course, the goal is to get to a point where for more and more of these types of issues, you don't need to wake up the human at all.
turns.zh: 那个 Claude 可以决定：这是噪音还是真的？这只是第一道门。第一道门是：是噪音还是真的？如果是噪音，那么我们真正试图做的是避免人类被打扰或被叫醒或其他什么。所以我们开始这样做，我们节省了大量人类时间，这些时间本来会花在调查最终是噪音的事情上。然后当它说“好的，这是真的”，在这种情况下，它将页面升级给人类，人类会进来开始查看。但在我们等待人类进来开始查看的那段时间里，Claude 也会开始查看并弄清楚我能做些什么来修复这个问题。通常当人类——特别是如果是半夜有人被叫醒——当他们到达笔记本电脑时，Claude 已经诊断了问题并有了推荐的修复方案，甚至可能已经开始采取一些行动，人类只需要说：“是的，谢谢，听起来很棒。”当然，目标是达到这样一个点：对于越来越多这类问题，你根本不需要叫醒人类。

ts.sec: Agents in Slack and production access

turns.en: Even if it's a real issue, it's something that Claude will hopefully just handle in a way that we can trust, and you don't have to wake anybody up. But we're not quite there yet. For now, we mostly just have the question of: is it noise or is it not, when a page comes in? And that has saved us a lot of time, which is great.
turns.zh: 即使它是个真问题，希望 Claude 也能以我们可以信任的方式处理掉，你不需要半夜叫醒任何人。但我们还没到那一步。目前我们主要只是判断：当一条告警进来时，它是噪音还是不是？这已经帮我们省了很多时间，很棒。

turns.en: So it's very clear how I think, and it's now clear in my head how engineers push to production. It's a lot of difference. You can now talk in Slack and with an agent steer it. It seems like a lot of work can be done. For non-engineers — product folks, design folks, just people who, by training, before this job, didn't push their code to production — do they also push out code into production by chatting, by creating features, by tweaking there? Or is the accountability typically still with an engineer, if it's a system that is not just a standalone small website that the marketing team owns, but inside the core of the core product? Can they already push to production? Do they push to production?
turns.zh: 所以我的思路很清楚，现在我脑子里也清楚了工程师是怎么把代码推到生产环境的。差别很大。你现在可以在 Slack 里说话，让一个智能体去操控它。看起来很多工作都能完成。那对于非工程师——产品的人、设计的人，就是那些在受训背景上、在这份工作之前从没把代码推到生产环境的人——他们也能通过聊天、通过创建功能、通过在那儿调整，把代码推到生产环境吗？还是说，如果这不是营销团队拥有的那种独立小网站，而是核心产品里的核心系统，责任通常仍然在工程师身上？他们现在能推生产了吗？他们真的在推生产吗？

turns.en: They can.
turns.zh: 他们可以。

turns.en: And so it's interesting, because you kind of mentioned this — oh, marketing site, you know, is maybe the canonical example of the place in the past where you would have said, okay, a product manager or designer can push to production and everyone feels okay about that, and they let that happen. I would just say the line of what goes in that category of 'we feel okay about that' is shifting over. So a really good example is we have a developer console. We have a user experience for developers who are building on the APIs, where you get your API keys and do your monitoring and all these sorts of things. We recently released a feature in the developer console that gives you diagnostics on your prompt caching. Prompt caching is really, really important with our APIs. You can save a lot of money and you can have a much better latency story if you're able to get a higher cache hit rate. We're starting to build more features that help engineers understand: am I getting a high cache hit rate? And if not, what might be happening, and what might I be able to do about it? And so we built that feature into the API. If you get a cache miss, then the response will kind of tell you why. We also built a dashboard into the developer console to help you see and understand what your rates are and what might be happening. And all of that was built by a product manager and pushed to production within our developer console.
turns.zh: 这很有意思，因为你提到了——营销网站，你知道，那可能是过去最典型的例子：你会说，好吧，产品经理或设计师可以推生产，大家都觉得没问题，就让他们这么做了。我想说的是，属于“我们觉得没问题”这个类别的边界正在移动。一个很好的例子是我们有一个开发者控制台。我们为在 API 上构建东西的开发者提供了一套用户体验，你在那里获取 API 密钥、做监控等等。我们最近在开发者控制台发布了一个功能，给你提供关于提示缓存的诊断。提示缓存对我们的 API 来说非常非常重要。如果你能获得更高的缓存命中率，你可以省很多钱，延迟表现也会好得多。我们开始构建更多功能，帮助工程师理解：我是否获得了高缓存命中率？如果没有，可能发生了什么，我能做些什么？所以我们把这个功能建进了 API。如果你遇到缓存未命中，响应会告诉你原因。我们还在开发者控制台里建了一个仪表盘，帮你查看和理解你的命中率是多少、可能发生了什么。而这一切都是由一位产品经理构建并推送到我们开发者控制台的生产环境的。

turns.en: Yeah, and so maybe, you know, we're not quite at the place where a core change to the core API is something that we would have a product manager or designer doing directly or spending time on. But for something like this, where it's like we can have a diagnostic dashboard that helps you think about your prompt caching and that's a great user experience for people — you know, the product manager who was working on this was obviously a relatively technical product manager, but he was kind of like, do I really need to bother an engineer for this? I don't think so. And of course we had engineers who could review the code and who could be involved and make sure that it was going to be high quality and things like this. But the actual implementation was that product manager and his Claude in Slack going back and forth and getting that thing built. And it's a really high quality feature, and it was totally built by a product manager.
turns.zh: 是的，所以也许，你知道，我们还没到那种程度：对核心 API 做核心改动，会让产品经理或设计师直接去做或花时间在上面。但像这样的事情——我们可以有一个诊断仪表盘，帮你思考你的提示缓存，对人们来说是很棒的用户体验——你知道，做这个的产品经理显然是个相对技术型的产品经理，但他当时想的是：我真的需要为这个去麻烦工程师吗？我觉得不用。当然我们有工程师可以审查代码、可以参与进来，确保它会高质量等等。但实际的实现就是那位产品经理和他 Slack 里的 Claude 来回沟通，把那个东西建出来的。这是一个质量很高的功能，而且完全是由一位产品经理构建的。

turns.en: But is it safe to say that the person who pushes to production in the end is the one accountable? It sounds like this product manager — if something would have gone wrong, or some numbers would have looked funny — this person would have absolutely taken full accountability, fixed it, figured out how to fix it. Because I think that's a bit of a differentiation — product managers to some extent have always been the ones owning the outcome. They just didn't have the tools to write the code. But in the end, often — I remember so many stories — a product manager, you know, we do the project, engineers build it, we want to ship it, or we show it to the product manager, and the product manager is like, hang on, that's not exactly how I was thinking. And the team was always connected in terms of product manager and engineers — it was shared accountability, if you will, or responsibility.
turns.zh: 但能不能说，最终推送到生产环境的人就是负责的人？听起来这位产品经理——如果出了什么问题，或者某些数字看起来奇怪——这个人绝对会承担全部责任，修好它，想办法解决。因为我觉得这有点区别——产品经理在某种程度上一直就是拥有结果的人。他们只是没有写代码的工具。但最终，经常——我记得很多故事——产品经理，你知道，我们做项目，工程师构建，我们想发布，或者我们给产品经理看，产品经理就说，等等，这不完全是我想要的。团队一直是连在一起的，产品经理和工程师——可以说是共同担责，或者共同负责。

turns.en: Yeah. I think it's pretty similar. I think it's like the team that owns the system is still ultimately the team that's getting paged when something goes wrong with that system, and they're jumping in and they're figuring out what went on. Like in the past you would always have times when an engineer from a different team might be trying to get something done and they'd kind of come into a part of the codebase owned by another team and they'd make some changes, right? And if something went wrong there, how does that get handled? It's like, well, something in that system that's owned by the team over here broke, and so the team over here that owns it gets paged, right? And then they might say, oh, this change was made recently by this person on this other team. Let me page them in and ask them questions about the thing, right? But ultimately the team that owns the system is responsible for keeping it high quality. And so the engineer over here that came in probably got code review from that team or got alignment in some form from that team, right? Because their job is to make that system high quality. I think all of that is exactly the same. So if that experience around cache diagnostics in our developer console had an issue, the team that owns our developer console, which is our developer experience team, is a team that would get paged, right? And then they might say, oh, there's something funky going on in this cache diagnostics thing that, you know, we know this product manager over here was part of building. And so we'll go page him and ask him for help thinking about this, because he might have details that this team doesn't have.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得挺相似的。我觉得拥有系统的团队，最终仍然是当系统出问题时被叫醒的团队，他们跳进来弄清楚发生了什么。就像过去总会有这样的情况：另一个团队的工程师可能想完成某件事，他们进入另一个团队拥有的代码库的一部分，做了一些改动，对吧？如果那里出了问题，怎么处理？就是，这边团队拥有的系统里某个东西坏了，所以拥有它的这边团队被叫醒，对吧？然后他们可能会说，哦，这个改动是另一个团队的某个人最近做的。让我把他叫进来，问问关于这件事的问题，对吧？但最终，拥有系统的团队负责保持它的高质量。所以这边进来的工程师大概从那个团队得到了代码审查，或者以某种形式从那个团队得到了对齐，对吧？因为他们的工作就是让那个系统保持高质量。我觉得这一切都完全一样。所以如果我们开发者控制台里那个缓存诊断的体验出了问题，拥有我们开发者控制台的团队——也就是我们的开发者体验团队——就是会被叫醒的团队，对吧？然后他们可能会说，哦，这个缓存诊断的东西有点怪，我们知道这位产品经理参与了构建。所以我们会去叫他，请他帮忙想想，因为他可能有一些这个团队没有的细节。

turns.en: But from that perspective, you kind of have to extrapolate that out to a point where now we have agents that aren't necessarily being orchestrated by a human, right? Like, get the SDK version bumped, or the CI went red and let's have an agent just catch that and fix it and make it go green, right? Any of these changes that don't have a human in the loop — the accountability question gets really funny. But I think ultimately it's the system that is owned by a specific team having an issue. It's that team's goal to keep that system high quality.
turns.zh: 但从那个角度，你得把它外推到这样一个程度：现在我们有智能体，不一定由人来编排，对吧？比如，把 SDK 版本升一下，或者 CI 变红了，让一个智能体直接接住、修好、让它变绿，对吧？任何这些没有人在环里的改动——责任问题就变得很滑稽。但我觉得最终，是某个特定团队拥有的系统出了问题。保持那个系统高质量，就是那个团队的目标。

turns.en: And so they're the ones who are going to be dealing with it even if it's an agent with no human involved at all, right? That made some change. It's like they're doing what they need to do to keep their system high quality.
turns.zh: 所以即使是一个完全不需要人类参与的智能体做出了某种改变，他们也是要处理这个问题的人，对吧？就像他们在做必要的事情来保持系统高质量。

turns.en: And I also think that's why we go back to we still have these two pizza teams, right? Like you still have a set of humans who understand the system, they're accountable for the system because changes might come in in any number of ways. It might be a product manager, it might be an ambient agent, right? Like and you still got to keep it high quality.
turns.zh: 我也认为这就是为什么我们回到我们仍然有这些两个披萨团队，对吧？就像你仍然有一组人理解这个系统，他们对系统负责，因为变化可能以多种方式出现。可能是产品经理，可能是环境智能体，对吧？就像你仍然要保持高质量。

turns.en: It is really refreshing to me to hear that you're saying your teams own systems.
turns.zh: 听到你说你的团队拥有系统，这真的让我耳目一新。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Here's how a team operates. Like I think we mentioned teams more in this conversation than others, but sounds like you're really observing or believing that like teams are kind of like so critical for like high quality products, systems or long living ones maybe.
turns.zh: 这就是团队的运作方式。我想我们在这次对话中提到的团队比其他人多，但听起来你真的观察到或相信团队对于高质量的产品、系统或长期存在的系统来说至关重要。

turns.en: Yeah, and I just don't think that that part has changed at least yet, right? And maybe over time you could say that that team could be a little bit smaller or something, right? Because they have more and more agents that are helping them and maybe, you know, like the team that's getting paid when something goes wrong is actually like the agents get paid first and most of the time the agents know what's going on, right? And I think over time that will change, but I still think there's some units of a set of humans who are accountable for a system operating the way that it's meant to and accomplishing its goals and doing all of those sorts of things that however bigger small that unit is, like that's ultimately who cares the most when something is going wrong and and they're the ones who are fixing it.
turns.zh: 是的，我只是不认为那部分已经改变了，至少目前还没有，对吧？也许随着时间的推移，你可能会说那个团队可以小一点之类的，对吧？因为他们有越来越多的智能体在帮助他们，也许，你知道，当出现问题时，实际上智能体会先得到报酬，大多数时候智能体知道发生了什么，对吧？我认为随着时间的推移，这种情况会改变，但我仍然认为有一些由一组人组成的单位，他们对系统按预期运行、实现其目标以及做所有这些事情负责，无论这个单位是大是小，最终当出现问题时，他们是最关心的，也是他们在修复问题。

turns.en: Now we talked so much about the different systems and different clouds and there's a durable cloud and the ones that you're spinning off. A term that is going around the industry, you've heard it so many times is software factory. What do you think about the name software factory and do you think what you're doing or how Anthropic is running could be described as such?
turns.zh: 现在我们谈了很多关于不同系统和不同云的事情，有一个持久云和你们正在剥离的云。业界流传的一个术语，你已经听过很多次了，就是软件工厂。你对软件工厂这个名字有什么看法？你认为你们正在做的事情或者 Anthropic 的运作方式可以这样描述吗？

turns.en: Yeah, it's really interesting. We I haven't really heard us use the term internally, but I do think that the spirit of what it's talking about is very much something that we are doing at Anthropic.
turns.zh: 是的，这真的很有趣。我们，我还没有真正听到我们在内部使用这个术语，但我确实认为它所谈论的精神正是我们在 Anthropic 所做的。

turns.en: You're definitely doing it.
turns.zh: 你们肯定在这样做。

turns.en: Yeah, we're definitely doing it, but we haven't called it software factory for I'm not sure why, but yeah, that's how we're working. It's very much like you want to get a change end to end and to production, right? You've got the agents that are actually making the change, you've got agents that are verifying the change, you've got agents that are taking the first pass at code review, maybe they're doing the whole code review, right? And then they're deploying to production and then once something is in production, you have monitoring, right? Like we recently started experimenting with actually like QA agents that are just
turns.zh: 是的，我们肯定在这样做，但我们没有称之为软件工厂，我不确定为什么，但是的，这就是我们的工作方式。这非常像你想要端到端地将变更投入生产，对吧？你有实际进行变更的智能体，你有验证变更的智能体，你有进行第一轮代码审查的智能体，也许他们做整个代码审查，对吧？然后他们部署到生产环境，一旦某些东西进入生产环境，你就有监控，对吧？比如我们最近开始试验实际上像 QA 智能体，它们只是

turns.en: External QA agents like trying to
turns.zh: 外部 QA 智能体，像是试图

turns.en: Yeah, they're just ambience and they have like a human written here's how the system is meant to work, right? And then they go and they're just constantly, you know, hammering on that thing and making sure that it works the way that it's meant to and then they're putting up pull requests if something is broken, right? And all of those different parts of the like get a change into production and then keep a system high quality once it's in production and then we talked about it on call too, right? Like taking the first page. All of those things are things that as much as we can we're trying to have agents take on more and more and more of that work so that the humans can spend their time on the higher quality work that needs to happen in order to get systems built and running at high quality.
turns.zh: 是的，它们只是环境智能体，它们有像人类写的那样“这是系统应该如何工作”，对吧？然后它们去不断地，你知道，敲打那个东西，确保它按预期工作，然后如果有东西坏了，它们就提交拉取请求，对吧？所有这些不同的部分，比如将变更投入生产，然后一旦进入生产就保持系统高质量，然后我们在 on-call 中也谈到了，对吧？比如接第一页。所有这些事情都是我们尽可能让智能体承担越来越多的工作，这样人类就可以把时间花在需要发生的高质量工作上，以便构建和运行高质量的系统。

turns.en: Now like what you're talking about is well you're on the cloud platform team which is an interesting name because externally it makes sense as a platform but platform teams can also be the ones that have built developer tools or infra tools and so on. These feedback loops the categorizing of different pull requests is this done by a platform team or each team deciding how they will build the tools?
turns.zh: 现在就像你所说的，你在云平台团队，这是一个有趣的名字，因为对外部来说作为一个平台是有意义的，但平台团队也可以是构建开发者工具或基础设施工具等的团队。这些反馈循环，不同拉取请求的分类，是由平台团队完成的，还是每个团队决定他们如何构建工具？

turns.en: It's a really good question. So we have a central infra org that's separate from my team and that team does infra across research and inference and product and all the different things and so we kind of have a version of an infra team within the platform team that specifically focus on product but they collaborate a lot with the centralized infra team. And so a lot of the work that's happened to try to make everybody more efficient has come from a developer acceleration team that sits within that central infra team. So they built Scion that we talked about recently and yeah
turns.zh: 这是一个非常好的问题。所以我们有一个独立于我的团队的中心基础设施组织，那个团队做跨研究、推理、产品和所有不同事物的基础设施，所以我们有点在平台团队内有一个基础设施团队的版本，专门专注于产品，但他们与中心基础设施团队合作很多。因此，很多试图让每个人更高效的工作来自一个位于中心基础设施团队内的开发者加速团队。所以他们构建了我们最近谈到的 Scion，是的

turns.en: New source control.
turns.zh: 新的源代码控制。

turns.en: So they've done a lot of really really incredible work to figure out how we go through this period of like insane number of changes that everybody's trying to make and make these things at high quality. So that team has done that type of work and then on top of this we actually have a team within platforms called platform acceleration that is collaborating a lot with the overall developer acceleration team, but their job is to just think specifically about platform and our team and the work that we're doing and the tools that we might want to have in order to make our teams move fast. And so, for example, I just mentioned that QA agent that's running like the platform acceleration team built that or you know, like I briefly mentioned CI. When CI goes red, we have agents that go and fix the tests and humans most of the time don't have to be in the loop. That's something the platform acceleration team built on top of a lot of the tools that were built by the developer acceleration team. And so, there's that. And then the last category I would just say is every engineer who's doing work is like totally empowered to think about all the things they could be doing that would make their lives better and their team.
turns.zh: 所以他们做了很多非常非常了不起的工作，弄清楚我们如何度过这段每个人都在尝试进行大量变更的时期，并高质量地完成这些事情。所以那个团队做了那类工作，然后在此基础上，我们实际上在平台内有一个名为平台加速的团队，他们与整体开发者加速团队合作很多，但他们的工作是专门考虑平台和我们的团队以及我们正在做的工作，以及我们可能想要拥有的工具，以便让我们的团队快速行动。所以，例如，我刚才提到的那个 QA 智能体，运行起来像是平台加速团队构建的，或者你知道，就像我简要提到的 CI。当 CI 变红时，我们有智能体去修复测试，大多数时候人类不需要介入。这是平台加速团队在开发者加速团队构建的许多工具之上构建的。所以，就是这样。然后最后一个类别我只想说，每个正在工作的工程师都被完全授权去思考他们可以做的所有事情，让他们的生活和团队变得更好。

turns.en: Lives better.
turns.zh: 生活更好。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Make things more efficient. And so, a lot of our most amazing tools that have, you know, helped teams do better work is just like some engineer who ran into some bottleneck that they thought was annoying and they were kind of inspired to go do something to fix it. And so, I would actually say on the whole, the number of human hours that go into the kind of meta work of tooling around the edges to make the work go faster has gotten I would say the balance has shifted. It's gotten higher as more work has become agentic, which is maybe counterintuitive because it's like you've got agents now who are doing so much of the work.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。让事情更高效。所以，我们许多最神奇的工具，你知道，帮助团队做得更好，就像某个工程师遇到了一些他们认为烦人的瓶颈，他们受到启发去做什么来修复它。所以，我实际上会说，总体而言，投入在边缘工具化的元工作以让工作更快的人类小时数已经增加了，我会说平衡已经转移。随着更多工作变得智能体式，它变得更高，这可能有点反直觉，因为就像你现在有智能体在做这么多的工作。

turns.en: And so that speeds people up, and they can just focus on the actual work itself. But I think because there's this whole world of tooling that you can create with these agents to push harder and harder on this goal of how many humans you need in the loop to get things done, everybody's really inspired by that problem, and everybody's spending a lot of time thinking about how can I take this workflow that was silly and I spent time on something that I probably didn't need to, and make that more automated or make that more agentic. So across all of those layers, we have people spending a lot of time on that.
turns.zh: 这样一来就加快了人们的速度，他们可以专注于实际工作本身。但我觉得，正因为你可以用这些智能体打造出一整套工具生态，不断朝“完成一件事到底需要多少人在环”这个目标施压，所有人都被这个问题激发，都在花大量时间思考：我怎样才能把这个本来很傻、我花了时间在其实没必要的事情上的工作流，变得更自动化、更智能体式。所以在所有这些层面上，都有很多人在花大量时间做这件事。

turns.en: Do I understand correctly that there is a developer—there are acceleration teams. I like that, because in the past these would have been called developer platform for AI, and I really like the acceleration part. But there are people working inside of platform acceleration or infra acceleration, and it seems their job—clearly their stated role or goal—is to make things more efficient for software engineers. But is it also true, what I'm picking up, that either by choice a lot of software engineers who are working in, let's say, product—they're working on a specific part of the product—are choosing to find ways to make their own work less repetitive, automated, to generally move more efficiently? Clearly they're running multiple agents—we're talking five, 10, or even more—figuring out how they can make those more efficient with tweaks. So there's a lot of experimentation playing around there.
turns.zh: 我理解得对吗——有一个开发者……有加速团队，我喜欢这个说法，因为过去这些会被叫作 AI 的开发者平台，但我真的很喜欢“加速”这个部分。不过确实有人在平台加速或基础设施加速团队里工作，看起来他们的工作——明确说他们的角色或目标——就是让软件工程师更高效。但我捕捉到的另一点是否也成立：很多做产品、比如负责产品某个具体部分的软件工程师，无论是出于自愿还是别的，都在想办法让自己的工作更少重复、更自动化、整体更高效？显然他们在跑多个智能体——五个、十个甚至更多——琢磨怎么通过微调让它们更高效。所以那里有大量实验和尝试。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And people can just kind of build what they want to build. A really cool example: some number of months ago we had someone on my team—not on platform acceleration, so his main job is not to do this type of work—who was thinking about how we have all these Slack-based agents that we spend a lot of our time with, and what is maybe the right form factor within Slack for somebody to be able to fire off a much, much, much more ambitious goal. And so he came up with this concept of a Slack channel that's dedicated to orchestrating a big multi-agent team in order to work towards some specific goal. So you would have a lot of instances of your Claude within that Slack channel, and that was all orchestrated with some tooling that helped the multi-agent team. This was before multi-agent had gotten better and better to the point where you don't really have to spend so much time thinking about exactly how the multi-agent system will orchestrate itself—let it do it on its own. But at the time it was all an experiment on how can we try to one-shot some really, really ambitious goal within a Slack channel with a team of agents working on that thing. And it's interesting because it ended up morphing into something that was more about persistent problems, like ambient problems that you might have. Maybe you have that team of agents just scanning for vulnerabilities in a codebase or something and just fixing them. And so the concept kind of changed over time, but it all started from just some engineer saying, let's experiment with the form factors here, and let's experiment with how we can have a multi-agent team do more ambitious work. And it wasn't his job, but it helped him do his job, and so that's what he spent his time on.
turns.zh: 对，正是这样。人们可以就建自己想建的东西。一个很酷的例子：几个月前，我团队里有个人——不在平台加速团队，所以他的主要工作不是做这类事——他在想，我们有这么多基于 Slack 的智能体，我们大量时间都花在上面，那么在 Slack 里，一个人要能发出一个宏大得多的目标，合适的形态是什么？于是他提出了一个概念：一个专门的 Slack 频道，用来编排一个大型多智能体团队，朝某个具体目标推进。于是你会在那个 Slack 频道里有很多个 Claude 实例，而这一切都由一些帮助多智能体团队的工具来编排。那是在多智能体变得足够好之前——好到现在你不太需要花那么多时间思考多智能体系统到底该如何自我编排，让它自己来就行。但当时这完全是个实验：我们能不能在一个 Slack 频道里，让一个智能体团队一次性搞定一个非常非常宏大的目标。有意思的是，它最终演变成了更偏向持续性问题的东西，比如你可能有的那些常驻问题。也许你让那个智能体团队去扫描代码库里的漏洞之类，然后直接修掉。所以这个概念随着时间变了，但一切都始于某个工程师说：我们来实验一下这里的形态，实验一下怎么让多智能体团队做更有野心的工作。这不是他的本职工作，但它帮他做好了自己的工作，所以他把时间花在了这上面。

turns.en: Speaking of the job in general, how is hiring changing? Felix Rieseberg, your colleague, wrote about how either his team or—I'm not sure if Anthropic decided that the coding interview doesn't give much signal. Just your org talking about the Claude platform—how are you hiring? How is it changing? What are you looking for? How are you verifying? Because hiring has always been difficult—you know when the person can do the job when they're doing the job, but beforehand there's a way we need to somehow filter.
turns.zh: 说到工作本身，招聘正在怎么变？你的同事 Felix Rieseberg 写过，他的团队或者——我不确定是不是 Anthropic——认定编程面试给不出多少信号。就你们这个组织、聊 Claude 平台这块——你们怎么招聘？在怎么变？你们看重什么？怎么验证？因为招聘一直很难——一个人能不能干这活，等他干上了才知道，但在此之前，我们总得有个办法筛选。

turns.en: It's a huge change.
turns.zh: 这是巨大的变化。

turns.en: It's a big change.
turns.zh: 是很大的变化。

turns.en: And it's interesting because I'm being pretty specific with the phrase phased out, because what happened was we were running a coding interview alongside—of course, we have interviews that test for technical design, or the ability to talk about a large technical project you worked on in the past, all the other signal that you get beyond just putting hands on keyboard and writing code. We found ourselves getting more and more to a point—I mean, it sounds obvious, but someone might not pass that coding interview, but they would crush all the rest of the interviews. And it's because they're not writing code by hand all of the time anymore. And so we found ourselves more and more of the time almost saying, ah, that's okay. And this is always a challenge in hiring—not every interview loop is perfect across the board, and you decide how do you get counter-signal and how do you decide ultimately that someone's going to be successful. And so on the coding interviews we were just finding that we weren't putting a ton of stock in them, because we kept saying, well, they might not be writing a ton of code by hand anymore. And so what we have done is we didn't just delete it. We've started to experiment with a bunch of different interviews that are basically coding-agent-driven interviews. So maybe it's reviewing code that was written by an agent, or reviewing a system design that was made by an agent, or building some system or building something using a coding agent. We're experimenting with a lot of these because we're basically trying to find the best way to really truly get signal on whether someone can use these tools really well to get work done. So very specifically, the part that used to test for coding, we're trying to replace with something that tests for the ability to work with agents to get work done. But the rest of the interview has stayed the same—thinking about technical design and the projects that you've worked on and all of those other pieces.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，我用“逐步淘汰”这个说法是相当具体的，因为实际情况是，我们一边在跑编程面试，一边当然也有测试技术设计的面试，或者考察你能否谈论过去做过的大型技术项目，以及除了动手敲键盘写代码之外你能获得的所有其他信号。我们发现自己越来越走到一个地步——听起来很明显，但有人可能过不了编程面试，却能把其余所有面试都碾压。这是因为他们不再一直手写代码了。于是我们越来越多地几乎是在说：啊，没关系。这在招聘中一直是个挑战——不是每个面试流程都处处完美，你得决定怎么获得反向信号、怎么最终判断一个人会成功。所以在编程面试上，我们只是发现我们并不太看重它，因为我们一直在说：嗯，他们可能不再手写大量代码了。所以我们做的并不是直接删掉它。我们开始尝试一系列不同的面试，基本上都是由编程智能体驱动的面试。比如，也许是审查一个智能体写的代码，或者审查一个智能体做的系统设计，或者用编程智能体搭建某个系统、构建某个东西。我们在大量尝试这些，因为基本上是在找最好的方式，真正获得信号：这个人能不能很好地用这些工具把活干完。所以具体来说，过去测试编程的那部分，我们正试图换成测试“能否与智能体协作完成工作”的内容。但面试的其余部分保持不变——考察技术设计、你做过的项目，以及所有其他环节。

turns.en: Yeah, because one thing with the coding interview—you'll notice as a hiring manager—the reason it was kind of convenient at every larger-size company is two reasons. One is it didn't really matter if a question leaked online, because it's not great when people know the question—they can come prepared and you'll get zero signal. That's one. And then the other thing: it was pretty easy to train a large number of interviewers on how to conduct this interview and get roughly equal signal, even if it's an early-career person or someone who hasn't had many interviews, or someone who has a lot of interviews.
turns.zh: 对，因为编程面试有一点——作为招聘经理你会注意到——它在每个规模较大的公司都挺方便，原因有两个。一是题目泄露到网上其实关系不大，因为当人们知道题目时就不妙了——他们可以有备而来，你就得到零信号。这是一点。另一点是，培训大量面试官如何开展这场面试、并获得大致相同的信号，是相当容易的，无论对方是早期职业者、没经历过多少面试的人，还是面试经验丰富的人。

turns.en: But also when I was a hiring manager and sat on the panels, the signal from the coding interview was always a little bit like—sometimes people will fail coding interviews and they will still get hired. So I feel it was the one that gave the least nuance. It was a zero or one that wasn't as precise anyway, because we know that even back then the data science and algorithm in the DSA interviews were not testing for the type of coding that we're doing day to day.
turns.zh: 但当我还是招聘经理并坐在面试小组里时，编程面试的信号总是有点像是——有时候人们会在编程面试中失败，但他们仍然会被录用。所以我觉得这是最缺乏细微差别的一个。它是个 0 或 1，反正也不那么精确，因为我们知道即使在当时，DSA 面试中的数据科学和算法也没有测试我们日常所做的那种编程。

turns.en: Right. Exactly.
turns.zh: 对。没错。

turns.en: So they were never perfect. But I think you do bring up a good point that whether an interview is successful—like a type of interview that you're going to run is successful—is not just about what's the exact signal that we're trying to get and can we get that signal? Some of it is can you trust it? Some of it is how hard is it, how onerous is it to have your team ready to grade that interview, right? And to score that interview and how hard is it to get more unbiased signal, right? Like a rubric that is pretty easy to stick to. And so this is why we're not just deleting the coding interview, but we're also not just like here's the exact thing that we're going to swap in instead. It's the reason why we're testing a bunch of different options for how we kind of hit where we want to hit on all of those different factors.
turns.zh: 所以它们从来都不是完美的。但我认为你确实提出了一个很好的观点：一次面试是否成功——比如你要进行的一种面试是否成功——不仅仅在于我们试图获得的确切信号是什么，以及我们能否获得那个信号？部分在于你能信任它吗？部分在于让你的团队准备好评分那次面试有多难、有多繁重，对吧？以及给那次面试打分有多难，还有获得更无偏的信号有多难，对吧？比如一个很容易坚持的评分标准。所以这就是为什么我们不只是删除编程面试，但也不是简单地说“这是我们要换入的确切东西”。这就是为什么我们正在测试一堆不同的选项，以在我们想要在所有那些不同因素上达到目标的地方达到目标。

turns.en: Once someone gets an offer and joins Anthropic, how do you think about things like leveling, performance reviews, promotions? Or do you think about this? And how has it changed? Because again, thinking back to like Stripe and Uber and Meta and all these places, this was such a big part of those companies. It was all figured out. I think the role wasn't changing as much, so we had a few—like, you know, 5, 10, 15 years of stability, if you will, and that was a huge part of it. You know, people were worried when there were people rejecting offers when they didn't get the title that they were hoping for, the level they were hoping for, and so on. How do you think of it inside of Anthropic?
turns.zh: 一旦有人拿到录用通知并加入 Anthropic，你如何看待职级、绩效评估、晋升之类的事情？或者你会考虑这些吗？它又是如何变化的？因为再次回想 Stripe、Uber、Meta 和所有这些地方，这是那些公司非常重要的一部分。一切都已经弄清楚了。我认为角色变化没那么大，所以我们有几年——比如 5 年、10 年、15 年的稳定期，如果你愿意这么说的话，那是很大的一部分。你知道，当有人因为没得到他们希望的头衔、他们希望的职级等等而拒绝录用通知时，人们会担心。你在 Anthropic 内部是怎么考虑这个的？

turns.en: Yeah, so we still do levels, we still do promotions, we still do performance reviews, we do all these things. The two things that are most different are: one, we've skewed much more senior. And so—
turns.zh: 是的，所以我们仍然有职级，我们仍然有晋升，我们仍然有绩效评估，我们做所有这些事情。最不同的两点是：第一，我们的员工资历偏资深得多。所以——

turns.en: Hiring, right?
turns.zh: 招聘，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And I think it was always easier as a manager to think about what success looks like at more junior levels where it's a little bit more uniform, I would say. As you get more senior, you find people owning totally different problem spaces and totally different systems, and it's a little bit harder to say what does good performance look like at some very senior level? But that's where we are right now.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我认为作为经理，思考初级职级的成功是什么样子总是更容易，因为那里更统一一些，我想说。随着你变得更资深，你会发现人们拥有完全不同的问題空间和完全不同的系统，要说什么是在非常资深级别上的良好绩效就有点难了。但这就是我们现在的处境。

turns.en: I think this typically happened at the staff and above levels. It was no longer uniform.
turns.zh: 我认为这通常发生在 staff 及以上级别。它不再统一了。

turns.en: Exactly. And I think what we're starting to grapple with is both when we're hiring and then once we have people in seat and you think about their levels, we used to use the proxy. Everything's about impact, right? It's like what impact have you had? Exactly. But it's interesting because we used to use a proxy of, you know, like an effort that took a certain amount of time is maybe a proxy for how complex that effort might have been, right? Like you might say somebody who's like some senior level, right? Like we do the—we don't have titles. We're all member of technical staff and so it's all like numeric levels. But someone at a pretty high numeric level might have in their past company or in their current company worked on something that took, you know, two years, right? And then you say this person led this two-year-long effort. Like that's so complex. And now it's like, well, the thing that could take two years—like, you know, migrating the API from Python to Rust—someone leading that in a matter of five to six months is what we would have in the past said, oh, this is like a two-year effort. But then the complexity bar is different too, right? And so a lot of things have changed. And so we're kind of constantly iterating on how do we get a sense for the complexity of the work that somebody does. But ultimately the fallback is always just impact because you're able to look at something like that migration and say, okay, great, we saved this amount of CPU and our latency got this much better and all these different things and we avoided incidents and all of this, right? And you can kind of qualitatively look at the work somebody did and say they had to coordinate across all these teams and they did that really well, right? And these are the measures that we now look at to be able to understand seniority within our team. And it's gotten just harder because it used to be much easier and more deterministic, especially at lower levels. But all to say those main things, the idea of levels and promotions and performance reviews have all stayed the same because we're still operating a team that people who have careers and they're growing and they're doing all these things, right? And it's important to us to make sure that that is still a good process for people.
turns.zh: 没错。我认为我们开始应对的是，无论是在招聘时，还是当人们入职后你考虑他们的职级时，我们过去使用代理指标。一切都在于影响力，对吧？就像你产生了什么影响？没错。但有趣的是，我们过去使用一个代理指标，比如一项花费一定时间的工作可能是该工作复杂程度的代理指标，对吧？比如你可能会说某个资深级别的人，对吧？我们做的是——我们没有头衔。我们都是技术员工成员，所以都是数字职级。但一个数字职级相当高的人可能在他们过去的公司或现在的公司做过耗时两年的东西，对吧？然后你说这个人领导了这个为期两年的工作。那太复杂了。而现在情况是，可能耗时两年的东西——比如把 API 从 Python 迁移到 Rust——有人在五到六个月内领导完成，我们过去会说，哦，这像是两年的工作。但复杂度的标准也不同了，对吧？所以很多事都变了。所以我们不断迭代，如何感知某人工作的复杂度。但最终的后备始终是影响力，因为你可以看像那次迁移这样的事情说，好的，很好，我们节省了这么多 CPU，延迟改善了这么多，以及所有这些不同的事情，我们避免了事故等等，对吧？你可以定性地看某人做的工作，说他们必须跨所有这些团队协调，而且做得非常好，对吧？这些是我们现在用来理解团队内资历的衡量标准。它变得更难了，因为过去容易得多，也更确定，尤其是在较低职级。但总而言之，那些主要的东西，职级、晋升和绩效评估的概念都保持不变，因为我们仍然在运营一个团队，人们有职业生涯，他们在成长，他们在做所有这些事情，对吧？对我们来说，确保这对人们来说仍然是一个好的流程很重要。

turns.en: One thing about performance reviews is that it's not just about performance necessarily, but it's often most companies run every six months where it's a place where people get feedback, typically from their manager, because managers are now forced to like, okay, you need to tell people constructive feedback, positive feedback, and so on. How does feedback work inside of teams or between teams or between individuals?
turns.zh: 关于绩效评估的一点是，它不一定只是关于绩效，但通常大多数公司每六个月运行一次，这是一个人们获得反馈的地方，通常来自他们的经理，因为经理现在被迫要说，好吧，你需要告诉人们建设性反馈、积极反馈等等。在团队内部、团队之间或个人之间，反馈是如何运作的？

turns.en: Yeah. I would say not that different than it ever used to work. We still do—I mean, I guess every manager has their own philosophy. My manager philosophy is if I get to a performance review time and I tell you something, some bit of feedback that feels super surprising to you, then I messed up.
turns.zh: 是的。我会说和以往运作方式没有太大不同。我们仍然做——我的意思是，我猜每个经理都有自己的理念。我的经理理念是，如果我到了绩效评估的时候，告诉你一些让你感到非常惊讶的反馈，那么我搞砸了。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Like you should have heard that from me more in real time. And so we still hold philosophies like this, but then when it comes to collecting feedback from other people, for example, I think again really similar, you know, like if someone comes to me and has got feedback for someone on my team, often it's like, is this something you can talk to them about directly, right? So we're not playing telephone and people can have open conversations. But at performance review time, we have the process of you can request feedback from peers or you can just kind of submit feedback. One of the nice things about Anthropic is our feedback is mostly transparent.
turns.zh: 比如你应该更实时地从我这里听到那个。所以我们仍然坚持这样的理念，但当涉及到从其他人那里收集反馈时，比如，我认为再次非常相似，你知道，就像如果有人来找我，对我团队中的某人有反馈，通常会是，这是你能直接和他们谈的事情吗，对吧？所以我们不玩传话游戏，人们可以进行开放的对话。但在绩效评估时，我们有流程，你可以向同事请求反馈，或者你可以直接提交反馈。Anthropic 的一个好处是我们的反馈大多是透明的。

turns.en: Yeah, like I've been at places in the past where the feedback that you give about somebody goes to their manager and they never see it, right? And when I was at Stripe, we kind of went back and forth on how all those things worked, but at Anthropic we err much more on the side of transparency and so people kind of see directly what...
turns.zh: 嗯，我以前待过一些地方，你给别人的反馈会直接到他们的经理那里，而他们本人永远看不到，对吧？在 Stripe 的时候，我们来回讨论过这些事该怎么运作，但在 Anthropic，我们更倾向于透明，所以人们能直接看到……

turns.en: There should be fewer surprises.
turns.zh: 应该少一些意外。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.en: Yeah. We can see that there is and we touched on this, but there's an identity crisis with software engineers. And you recently reflected on this in writing, and I'll quote you a little bit for this. You wrote, this is for the engineers feeling an identity crisis because they think their knowledge and skills won't be important, even though your skills can be the difference in whether or not these complex problems will be tackled. And then you gave for example multi-agent systems as an example.
turns.zh: 是的。我们能看出确实存在，而且我们之前也提到过，软件工程师存在身份危机。你最近在文章里反思了这一点，我引用一下你的话。你写道，这是写给那些感到身份危机的工程师的，因为他们认为自己的知识和技能不再重要，尽管你的技能可能决定这些复杂问题能否被解决。然后你举了多智能体系统作为例子。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Can you share like what you're seeing in terms of like the identity crisis and like where you see the light at the end of the tunnel?
turns.zh: 你能分享一下你看到的身份危机是什么样，以及你认为隧道尽头的光在哪里吗？

turns.en: Yeah. And we talked a little bit earlier about this idea of what do you get joy out of when you're doing this type of work? And I think especially for people who get a lot of joy out of you know, some ambitious problem is tackled, right? That those are the people who there's so much that is unsolved, that needs to get solved and there's just like an endless amount of joy that you can get out of spending the time on solving those problems. I think the people who are having a harder time are the people who are like my identity used to be that I like you know click clacked on my keyboard and I I wrote code and stuff got done from that perspective and the idea in writing that was mostly to try to spark some optimism of I'm really excited. I have a lot of optimism because there are huge problems that we want to tackle, right? Like yes, fine. It's the case that you no longer write individual lines of code, but what we want to have happen with AI is to get to a point where like diseases are getting cured, right? And you know, like really incredible feats can happen in in mechanical engineering and all of these other areas that we for a long time used to think were science fiction, right? But we can go and solve those problems. And I think what people kind of need to think about and focus on is people will often say like oh why why does this thing matter? Like agents will do it eventually or why does that thing matter? Like agents will do it eventually. But I think the point is in order to enable agents to be able to solve those problems, there's a lot of engineering problems that have to get tackled soon. And so big example being these multi-agent systems, right? Like you can have thousands of agents that are working together in order to solve a problem. We've heard from some customers really interesting examples like if you're working on curing a disease and you're working on maybe a drug that you want to make available in the market and you have to submit to the FDA your packet of here's why you should allow this drug to go in the market. An insane amount of time and energy and effort goes into each of those phases of getting all the way to a place where a drug is on the market. And what we've seen people starting to do is maybe you like build some system that's almost like it's almost like a Gantt chart, right? Like and and what happens is persistent agents are picking up the different pieces of the work and they're doing all the different pieces of the work and you might not have to have humans in the loop for a lot of the different parts of what's happening there. These things are only just starting to happen. Like think about the problems that you're solving and you're working with agents and like you're saying here individual agent go do that thing here you know, but now think about take the ambition level way way way up and have a team of agents just kind of go at it and get that thing done. What I'm hoping for people to understand is that's not going to happen if we don't solve engineering problems around security and engineering problems around infrastructure and identity and auth and all these different problems that you can't just let a huge team of agents go wild trying to solve these problems if you haven't solved some of these underlying engineering problems correctly first because we're never going to get there. We're never going to get to the place where the big team of agents solves the good problem. We're going to have problems first, right? Like bad problems having happened first and so idea being yes, agents can help us solve a lot of these problems now on the path to that, but we still need humans who have deep expertise in security and deep expertise in auth and infra and all these different pieces in order to create the right underlying systems so that those teams of agents can go and solve those big problems.
turns.zh: 是的。我们之前聊过，做这类工作时，你从什么中获得快乐？我认为尤其是那些从解决雄心勃勃的问题中获得很多快乐的人，他们面前有太多未解决的问题需要解决，投入时间解决这些问题能带来无尽的快乐。我觉得更艰难的是那些把身份认同建立在“我在键盘上敲敲打打写代码，然后事情就完成了”的人。我写那篇文章主要是想激发一些乐观情绪：我非常兴奋，也非常乐观，因为我们有巨大的问题想要解决。是的，你不再写单行代码了，但我们希望 AI 能达到治愈疾病的程度，对吧？在机械工程和其他领域，我们长期认为是科幻的惊人成就，现在我们可以去解决那些问题了。我认为人们需要思考和关注的是，人们常问“为什么这件事重要？智能体最终会做的”，但关键是，为了让智能体能够解决那些问题，有很多工程问题必须尽快解决。一个重要的例子就是多智能体系统：你可以有成千上万个智能体协同工作来解决问题。我们从一些客户那里听到了非常有趣的例子，比如你在研究治愈某种疾病，可能是一种你想推向市场的药物，你必须向 FDA 提交材料说明为什么应该允许这种药物上市。在药物上市的每个阶段，都投入了惊人的时间、精力和努力。我们看到人们开始做的是，构建一个几乎像甘特图一样的系统，然后持久性智能体接手不同的工作部分，完成所有不同的工作，很多环节可能不需要人类参与。这些事情才刚刚开始发生。想想你正在解决的问题，你与智能体合作，你说“单个智能体去做那件事”，但现在把雄心水平大大提高，让一个智能体团队去完成那件事。我希望人们理解的是，如果我们不解决安全、基础设施、身份和认证等工程问题，那就不可能实现。如果你没有先正确解决一些底层工程问题，你就不能放任一大群智能体疯狂地尝试解决这些问题，因为我们永远到不了那一步。我们永远到不了让大团队智能体解决好问题的那一步。我们会先遇到问题，坏问题会先发生。所以，是的，智能体现在可以在实现目标的路上帮助我们解决很多问题，但我们仍然需要拥有安全、认证和基础设施等深厚专业知识的人类来创建正确的底层系统，以便那些智能体团队能够去解决那些大问题。

turns.en: What you're talking about makes sense for anyone who is either working inside a place where they do have large AI budgets and and running lots of agents or in a frontier lab or something close, but like I do think that multi-agent systems are pretty far-fetched for more people who are you know engineers who still have the they have the max plan and that's all they can use. They cannot request an extension and so on, but even for for them to Tarik had a really good quote. I'll I'll also read him. He said it's a very weird thing happening right now. Technical people are sad because they're they think their skills are useless and people are desperately wishing they were more technical so they could use agents better.
turns.zh: 你说的对任何在有大量 AI 预算、运行大量智能体的地方工作的人，或者在前沿实验室或类似地方工作的人来说都说得通。但我确实认为多智能体系统对更多人来说相当遥远，比如工程师们仍然只有 Max 套餐，只能用那个，不能申请扩展等等。但即使对他们来说，Tarik 有一句很好的话，我也读一下。他说现在发生了一件很奇怪的事：技术人员很伤心，因为他们认为自己的技能没用了；而其他人拼命希望自己更懂技术，以便更好地使用智能体。

turns.en: Nice.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.en: I think you've seen this as well.
turns.zh: 我想你也看到了这一点。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: But there's this thing where when you talked about all the things that agents could do, cure diseases and all those things which I think would be amazing, but I have a more pressing need which is for example I'm going to be flying to London and I'm using the British Airways app and it is the bottom of airline apps. It is so beyond terrible. I'm just calling them out because they're objectively just please fix I'm hoping that someone listens on on the BA team, but there's a lot of just bad software that could be updated and there's a lot of decent software that can be great. A good example is Shopify. They're now rewriting so I feel for for even at all at these kind of like smaller ambition levels like it's awesome to hear that even the highest ambition levels you have way more ambition for engineering, but I think the lower levels there's also so much more ambition that would have said like oh we're not going to do it because it'll take years to rewrite or there's the expensing apps that have terrible user experience like all of these can now maybe just tackle the next like month in in in a matter of months not years or or decades.
turns.zh: 但有个事情，当你谈到智能体能做的所有事情，治愈疾病等等，我觉得那会很棒，但我有更紧迫的需求，比如我要飞伦敦，我用英国航空的 app，它是最差的航空公司 app，太糟糕了。我点名是因为客观上它就是这样，希望 BA 团队有人听到，请修复。有很多糟糕的软件可以更新，很多不错的软件可以变得很棒。Shopify 是个好例子，他们现在在重写。所以我觉得即使在那些较小的雄心层面上，听到你们在最高雄心层面上对工程有更大的雄心很棒，但我认为在较低层面上也有更多雄心，以前会说“哦我们不做，因为重写要几年”，或者费用报销 app 用户体验糟糕，所有这些现在也许可以在几个月内解决，而不是几年或几十年。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And I think it's all time scale, right? Like the world's hardest problems, we're maybe talking months, years out, right? But even in the coming weeks and single-digit months, all of these people who run these systems, these apps, whatever that could be, could be so much better. All you really need to do is raise your ambition level. And it's true that you might just have a Max plan and that's what you're working with, right? One of the cool things we did recently is Max plans come with API credits, and so you can go start to build these persistent agents on Cloud managed agents or whatever it might be that can go tackle harder problems as well. And so it's interesting because I think you're exactly right, that it's just a matter of continuously raising the level of ambition in any problem space that you're in. I was recently working with one of our AI for legal customers and they were talking about how, yes, the models today are incredibly good at reviewing a contract, right? Like that's kind of the main basic thing that you use AI for. But what they're starting to do is say, maybe AI can run an entire diligence process, right? Like something way, way, way, way more ambitious than anything that you previously would have thought about. And that's because you can build a more complex multi-agent system and you can have more orchestration happening and more work ultimately getting done. And that's the sort of thing where a user of that AI legal product is going to have a much better time if their job is to get a whole diligence process done. It used to be, like, I'm going to have the agents go do all these little pieces myself, but now you can kind of work with that thing and say, like, do the whole big ambitious thing all up front. And then the engineers at that AI legal company need to think about what they're going to have to build in order to enable the agents to go run a whole diligence process and make sure that it actually goes well. So I think that's what I mean, right? In any place, at any scale, if you raise the ambition level, there's still work that engineers are going to have to do in order to enable that elevated ambition. And we're not yet anywhere close to a point where it's like the human doesn't have to do anything and the agents will just figure it out, because it'll probably go wrong if all you're doing is leaving it fully to the expectation that agents will do it all without humans creating the right systems and guardrails and security and all the things underneath.
turns.zh: 对，完全正确。我觉得这全是时间尺度的问题，对吧？世界上最难的问题，我们可能在说几个月、几年之后，对吧？但即便在未来几周、个位数月份内，所有运行这些系统、这些应用的人，不管是什么，都可以好得多。你真正需要做的就是提高你的雄心水平。确实，你可能只有一个 Max 套餐，那就是你手头用的东西，对吧？我们最近做的一件很酷的事是，Max 套餐附带 API 额度，所以你可以开始在云端托管智能体之类的东西上构建这些持久化的智能体，去解决更难的问题。所以这很有意思，因为我觉得你说得完全对，关键就是在你所在的任何问题领域里不断提高雄心水平。我最近和我们的一个 AI 法律客户合作，他们在说，是的，今天的模型在审阅合同方面非常出色，对吧？这大概是你用 AI 做的最基本的事。但他们开始说，也许 AI 可以跑完整个尽职调查流程，对吧？这比你之前能想到的任何事情都要雄心勃勃得多。这是因为你可以构建更复杂的多智能体系统，可以做更多的编排，最终完成更多的工作。而这类事情，那个 AI 法律产品的用户，如果他们的工作是完成整个尽职调查流程，他们的体验会好得多。以前是，我要让智能体自己去做所有这些小片段，但现在你可以和那个东西协作，说，把整个大而雄心勃勃的事情一次性做完。然后，那家 AI 法律公司的工程师需要思考，他们需要构建什么，才能让智能体跑完整个尽职调查流程，并确保它真的顺利进行。所以我觉得这就是我的意思，对吧？在任何地方、任何规模，如果你提高雄心水平，工程师仍然需要做工作来实现那种更高的雄心。我们离人类什么都不用做、智能体自己就能搞定那个点还差得远，因为如果你只是完全指望智能体自己做完一切，而没有人去创建正确的系统、护栏、安全以及底下所有这些东西，那很可能会出问题。

turns.en: One thing that I've been a little bit thinking about, or trying to have a mental model for, is we call software engineering like engineering, and there's a debate of whether it's real engineering compared to like civil engineering and so on. But now that we're talking about building new infrastructure that, let's say, multi-agents can use, and there's this big challenge that we need to learn and build it, you would think like, okay, but what happens once we build it? Like we're done and there will be no software engineering needed. But what I am thinking of is civil engineering, like building a skyscraper. You would think, okay, the skyscraper is built. It's been a huge engineering feat. I don't know how we did it with these bricks that cannot really take that load, but we built this incredible thing. And you would think, once we built it, well, I guess there's no more jobs, right? Because the job is done. But then you realize, hang on, civil architects are very much in demand because that skyscraper needs maintenance. Sometimes they will be demolished and new ones built. And then once the first skyscraper is built in the world, guess what? I guess there's so many more of these. I'm wondering if we'll have more parallels to other types of engineering, because now we have different materials. Like this AI is a new material. We have deterministic code. We have non-deterministic AI. We need to glue them together. Once we get to the point where we are solving multi-agent systems, can you think in advance of where the work might be, where you and your team will keep working on?
turns.zh: 我一直在稍微思考的一件事，或者说试图建立的一个心智模型是，我们把软件工程叫作工程，并且有争论说它和土木工程等相比算不算真正的工程。但现在我们谈论的是构建新的基础设施，比如多智能体可以使用的基础设施，而且有一个巨大的挑战，我们需要学习并构建它。你可能会想，好吧，但一旦我们建成了呢？我们就完成了，不再需要软件工程了。但我想到的是土木工程，比如建摩天大楼。你可能会想，好吧，摩天大楼建成了。这是一项巨大的工程壮举。我不知道我们是怎么用这些承受不了那么低载荷的砖块做到的，但我们建成了这个不可思议的东西。你可能会想，一旦我们建成了，好吧，我想就没有更多工作了，对吧？因为工作完成了。但然后你意识到，等等，土木建筑师非常抢手，因为那座摩天大楼需要维护。有时它们会被拆除，建新的。然后一旦世界上第一座摩天大楼建成，你猜怎么着？我想会有更多这样的东西。我在想，我们是否会有更多与其他类型工程的相似之处，因为现在我们有不同的材料。AI 是一种新材料。我们有确定性代码。我们有非确定性 AI。我们需要把它们粘合在一起。一旦我们到了解决多智能体系统的阶段，你能提前想到工作可能在哪里，你和你的团队会继续在哪里工作吗？

turns.en: Yeah, and I completely agree with that. You complete your project, right? And then you have to maintain it, but also you have to, you should keep building on it. You should keep figuring out what is the next level of thing, what is the more ambitious thing. And I think something that we are hoping to have agents do, especially within our team, is the maintenance aspect, which is the part that is maybe a little less fun.
turns.zh: 是的，我完全同意。你完成了你的项目，对吧？然后你必须维护它，但你也必须、你应该继续在它上面构建。你应该继续弄清楚下一层次的东西是什么，更雄心勃勃的东西是什么。我觉得我们希望智能体去做的一件事，尤其是在我们团队里，就是维护方面，那部分可能没那么有趣。

turns.en: We never enjoyed it.
turns.zh: 我们从来都不喜欢它。

turns.en: Yeah, have agents do more and more and more of that.
turns.zh: 是的，让智能体越来越多地做这些。

turns.en: Call and document writing documentation.
turns.zh: 打电话和写文档。

turns.en: Exactly, right. So can agents take more of that type of work off of people's hands and then say, okay, great, we're going to go think about what is the more ambitious work that can go and get done. And I think from the perspective of just get more ambitious with problems, I think multi-agent systems and continuously more complex multi-agent systems are going to matter a lot. And I think there's a lot of capabilities around the edges of these models that will continue to have engineering problems. So really good examples are you continue to need better and better tooling for an agent to be able to interact with some external systems. So a few of the engineers on my team created MCP, and there's some of the core maintainers of MCP continuing to evolve that standard, I think is really important. But another set of folks that we're working with are thinking about MHS, the model hardware standard, which is this idea of how can we have agents interacting with lab equipment or robotics, right? And stuff in the physical world. And I think that is all such early stages, right? And so if you think about as AI is going to expand from just self-contained systems that can solve really great problems in software, you're going to get more into hardware and you're going to get more into just even more complex systems that are going to need more solutions to more problems, right? And so I think we're just nowhere close to a world where there's not going to be anything left for the humans to think about. I think there's going to be a lot more time and a lot more of these problems that we'll need to get solved first.
turns.zh: 完全正确。所以智能体能不能把更多这类工作从人们手中接过去，然后说，好吧，太好了，我们要去思考能完成哪些更雄心勃勃的工作。而且我觉得，从让问题更雄心勃勃的角度看，多智能体系统以及持续更复杂的多智能体系统会非常重要。我觉得这些模型周边还有很多能力会持续带来工程问题。很好的例子是，你持续需要越来越好的工具，让智能体能够与某些外部系统交互。所以我团队里的几位工程师创建了 MCP，MCP 的一些核心维护者继续演进那个标准，我觉得这非常重要。但我们在合作的另一批人在思考 MHS，即模型硬件标准，这个想法是我们如何让智能体与实验室设备或机器人交互，对吧？以及物理世界中的东西。我觉得这些都还处于非常早期的阶段，对吧？所以如果你想想，随着 AI 从仅仅解决软件中很棒问题的自包含系统扩展出去，你会更多地进入硬件，你会更多地进入甚至更复杂的系统，这些系统需要更多问题的更多解决方案，对吧？所以我觉得我们离一个人类没什么可思考的世界还差得远。我觉得还需要更多时间，还需要先解决更多这类问题。

turns.en: What's your mental model about this, I guess, new software engineering job now that we have AI agents, we have multi-agent, we have all these tools, versus the old job that existed until agents showed up?
turns.zh: 你对这个的心智模型是什么，我猜，现在有了 AI 智能体、多智能体、所有这些工具，新的软件工程工作，与智能体出现之前存在的旧工作相比？

turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I think so much of it is coordination.
turns.zh: 是的，我是说，我觉得很大一部分是协调。

turns.en: It's getting teams and people on the same page. It's making agents get on the same page and get stuff done. I think it's really zooming out and understanding the mechanics of how you go from idea to reality on something, and you can offload a lot of the pieces of stuff that needs to happen to agents. But the coordination web that has to happen to make something really get shipped, and make something get shipped at high quality, there's just still so much there. There's so much that people are spending their time on that are important. And the ideas in the first place are important to you. And so I think those are the things that are going to matter a lot. And then I think especially in the near term, there's going to be really deep expertise that is really important, whether it's security or other fields like that that are right now feeling some challenges as a result of the technology and the things that are happening, where I think people can and should go deeper than they maybe otherwise would have in some of these domains that are starting to matter more than they did previously. So there's still a lot to learn and there's still a lot to solve, and I think there's still a lot of coordination to do in order to get those problems solved.
turns.zh: 关键在于让团队和人们达成共识，让智能体之间达成共识并把事情做成。我认为真正的重点是跳出来看，理解从想法到落地这件事的运作机制。你可以把很多需要完成的环节交给智能体，但要让某样东西真正交付出去、并且以高质量交付，背后那张协调网络依然有太多工作要做。人们花时间做的很多事情都很重要，最初的想法对你来说也很重要。所以我认为这些才是真正重要的东西。尤其是在近期，深厚的专业能力会非常重要，不管是安全还是其他领域，这些领域现在正因为技术和正在发生的事情而面临一些挑战。我认为人们可以也应该在这些领域比以往钻得更深，因为这些领域正变得比过去更重要。所以还有很多要学、还有很多要解决，而且我认为要解决这些问题还需要大量协调。

turns.en: It sounds like what you're saying is there's little to no downside as you're building things — hey, raise your ambition levels — but as you're building and using agents more, learn with them, get deeper. And especially — and we mentioned some of the areas — security is obviously a huge one right now. Like everything is changing. You can become a human expert in this area relatively quickly. And maybe you shouldn't — and that security might be one of reliability, or just your own domain, whatever your domain you're working in, right?
turns.zh: 听起来你的意思是，在构建东西的过程中几乎没有坏处——嘿，把野心提高一点——但在构建和使用智能体的过程中，要和它们一起学习、钻得更深。尤其是——我们提到了一些领域——安全现在显然是个大领域。一切都在变。你可以相对快速地成为这个领域的人类专家。也许你不该这么做——而那个安全可能指的是可靠性，或者就是你自己的领域，不管你在哪个领域工作，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And maybe it's not just to solve today's problems, right? Like maybe don't go become a security expert in order to solve one problem that's directly in front of you, because maybe that's not the best use of your time because an agent can figure it out and do it. But you can kind of extrapolate and see how some of the problems we're starting to experience are going to get more complex over time, right? And so you're going to want to be someone who can wrap your head around these things and see ahead and see around those corners and get in front of those things before they become more problematic. And again, agents can help with all of this for sure, but I still think that we're all going to be very deeply reliant on humans who care a lot about these things and have a lot of deep expertise to think about getting ahead of them.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。而且也许不只是为了解决今天的问题，对吧？也许不要为了眼前某一个具体问题就去成为安全专家，因为那可能不是你时间的最佳用法，智能体可以搞定并完成它。但你可以外推一下，看到我们开始遇到的一些问题会随着时间变得更复杂，对吧？所以你会希望自己成为那种能把这些事情想明白、能预见前方、能绕过那些弯角、在事情变得更麻烦之前就提前应对的人。再说一次，智能体肯定能帮上忙，但我仍然认为我们都会非常依赖那些真正在乎这些事情、拥有深厚专业能力的人去思考如何提前应对。

turns.en: Thank you. And what's a book that you would recommend that you enjoyed, and why?
turns.zh: 谢谢。你推荐一本你喜欢的书吧，为什么？

turns.en: One book that I really enjoyed that I read recently was Project Hail Mary. And the movie was pretty good too. But I think right now is a fun moment to get out of the weeds of everything that we're spending our time on day to day. And a feel-good story is nice, but also a nice science fiction expand-your-brain sort of story is nice. And I think Project Hail Mary — they did an absolutely excellent job with the idea of, you know, you've got a human and you've got an alien who don't know how to communicate with each other and they've got to figure it out. And it's a cool story, but it's also relatable in the sense of what we're dealing with right now with AI.
turns.zh: 我最近读的一本很喜欢的书是《挽救计划》（Project Hail Mary）。电影也挺不错的。我觉得现在正是一个好时机，从我们每天埋头忙的事情里跳出来。一个让人感觉良好的故事很好，但一个能扩展大脑的科幻故事也很好。我觉得《挽救计划》在“你有一个人类和一个外星人，他们不知道怎么交流，必须想办法搞明白”这个点子上做得非常出色。这是个很酷的故事，但它在某种意义上也让人有共鸣，就像我们现在面对 AI 时的处境。

turns.en: Awesome. Katelyn, thanks so much.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Katelyn，非常感谢。

turns.en: Yeah, thank you for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们邀请我。

turns.en: This was very nice and informative.
turns.zh: 这次非常愉快，也很有收获。

turns.en: It was a lot of fun.
turns.zh: 非常有意思。

turns.en: I really enjoyed getting all these details from Katelyn, and thanks a lot to her for this conversation. If you'd like to get into more details about how Anthropic works, check out the Pragmatic Engineer deep dive, How Building Software is Changing at Anthropic, in the show notes below.
turns.zh: 我非常喜欢从 Katelyn 这里听到的这些细节，也非常感谢她参与这次对话。如果你想了解更多 Anthropic 如何运作的细节，可以看看节目笔记里 Pragmatic Engineer 的深度文章《Anthropic 的软件构建方式正在如何改变》。

turns.en: It's now becoming more of a trend to hear anyone and everyone moving to Rust inside of AI labs for their backend services. Katelyn explained the reason better than I've heard before. Python was too CPU intensive, there's now a CPU shortage, and the models have gotten really good at writing Rust code. Plus, Rust makes services as performant as possible, on par if you ported them to C++ or C, but Rust gives you memory safety and a verification feedback layer for agents. So it's overall a lot more agent-friendly.
turns.zh: 现在越来越成为一种趋势：AI 实验室里几乎所有人都在把后端服务迁移到 Rust。Katelyn 解释的原因比我之前听过的都好。Python 太吃 CPU，而现在 CPU 短缺，同时模型写 Rust 代码已经写得非常好了。另外，Rust 能让服务性能尽可能高，和移植到 C++ 或 C 相当，但 Rust 还提供内存安全，以及给智能体的验证反馈层。所以整体上它对智能体友好得多。

turns.en: Another interesting part was confirming that Anthropic has now fully dropped algorithmic coding interviews, and this feels like a big milestone because they are the first large company to publicly confirm that they've done so. Katelyn said that they saw more candidates doing well in every other interview, but bombing the data structures and algorithms one because they were no longer writing code by hand. Even though Anthropic dropped this interview, they don't have a perfect replacement, and they're trying out different interviews built around coding agents and agentic coding.
turns.zh: 另一个有趣的点是确认 Anthropic 现在已经完全取消了算法编程面试，这感觉是个重要的里程碑，因为他们是第一家公开确认这么做了的大公司。Katelyn 说，他们看到越来越多候选人在其他所有面试里表现很好，却在数据结构与算法那一轮崩掉，因为他们不再手写代码了。尽管 Anthropic 取消了这种面试，他们也没有完美的替代方案，正在尝试围绕编程智能体和智能体式编程设计不同的面试。

turns.en: My take is that most companies will drop the coding interview eventually, but in return, the hiring process will become a lot more subjective. The interview loops will become a lot more similar in subjectivity to how engineering manager or product manager hiring loops have been in the past.
turns.zh: 我的看法是，大多数公司最终都会取消编程面试，但作为交换，招聘流程会变得主观得多。面试流程的主观程度会越来越像过去工程经理或产品经理的招聘流程。

turns.en: One somewhat surprising learning was that product managers in Anthropic have pushed code to production. I've been asking around about this because at most companies, engineers still own shipping production code. Granted, PMs at Anthropic are very technical and often come from engineering backgrounds, so I do wonder if PMs shipping production code will be as commonplace as at Anthropic. I'm a bit skeptical, but it's a good one to note how it's happening inside of Anthropic. Also, don't forget that the people on call for these changes are still the software engineers.
turns.zh: 一个有点令人意外的发现是，Anthropic 的产品经理曾把代码推送到生产环境。我一直在四处打听这件事，因为在大多数公司，工程师仍然负责交付生产代码。当然，Anthropic 的产品经理非常懂技术，往往有工程背景，所以我确实怀疑“产品经理交付生产代码”会不会像在 Anthropic 那样普遍。我有点怀疑，但值得记下 Anthropic 内部是怎么发生的。另外别忘了，为这些变更值班待命的仍然是软件工程师。

turns.en: Another interesting part is how much of the onboarding changes inside of Anthropic. The onboarding guide is pretty much just ask Claude. Tido at OpenAI said the same thing — we had OpenAI's onboarding with Codex. One very important detail is that both at Anthropic and OpenAI, they connect pretty much all their systems into their own internal Claude/Codex instances, and so those AI agents will have far more context than most agents inside of other companies. Then again, this might be one more reason to connect your internal systems to the company internal agent. Just make sure that you're not leaking company IP to AI vendors.
turns.zh: 另一个有趣的点是 Anthropic 内部的入职流程变化有多大。入职指南基本上就是“问 Claude”。OpenAI 的 Tido 也说过同样的话——我们用 Codex 做 OpenAI 的入职。一个非常重要的细节是，在 Anthropic 和 OpenAI，他们几乎把所有系统都接入了自己内部的 Claude/Codex 实例，所以这些 AI 智能体拥有的上下文远多于其他公司内部的大多数智能体。话又说回来，这也许是另一个理由，让你把内部系统接入公司内部智能体。只是要确保不要把公司知识产权泄露给 AI 供应商。

consensus.en: Verifiability, not line-by-line reading, is what lets agents write production code safely.
consensus.zh: 可验证性而非逐行阅读，才是让智能体安全编写生产代码的关键。

consensus.en: Rust's compile-time checks make it ideal for agent-written code: fewer bugs, more trust.
consensus.zh: Rust 的编译期检查使其非常适合智能体写代码：更少 bug，更多信任。

consensus.en: Shadowing Python and Rust side by side until outputs match was the real source of truth.
consensus.zh: 让 Python 与 Rust 影子并行、直到输出一致，才是真正的真相来源。

consensus.en: Engineers now spend most time on coordination and alignment, far less on implementation.
consensus.zh: 工程师如今大部分时间花在协调与对齐上，实现工作大幅减少。

consensus.en: Two-pizza teams persist because humans must stay accountable for system quality.
consensus.zh: 两个披萨团队依然存在，因为必须有人对系统质量负责。

consensus.en: Agents now handle code review, CI fixes, on-call triage, and QA, not just coding.
consensus.zh: 智能体现在不只写代码，还承担代码审查、CI 修复、值班分诊和 QA。

contrarian.en: You don't need to read most agent-written PRs if the outcome is verifiable.
contrarian.zh: 只要结果可验证，大多数智能体写的 PR 你并不需要读。

contrarian.en: Coding interviews were phased out because engineers no longer write code by hand.
contrarian.zh: 编码面试被淘汰，因为工程师不再手写代码。

contrarian.en: Choosing a language now barely matters; models absorb the learning and implementation cost.
contrarian.zh: 如今选哪种语言几乎不重要，模型吸收了学习与实现成本。

contrarian.en: Rebuilding the whole system from scratch mid-project became rational, not reckless.
contrarian.zh: 项目中途从零重写变得理性，而非鲁莽。

contrarian.en: A product manager shipped a production feature end-to-end without engineers writing it.
contrarian.zh: 一位产品经理端到端上线了生产功能，工程师并未动手写代码。

contrarian.en: More agentic work means more human hours on tooling, not fewer.
contrarian.zh: 智能体式工作越多，人类在工具上的投入反而越多，而非更少。
